title: Meta, Milan’s Pinacoteca di Brera, and EssilorLuxottica Expand Access to Art Through AI Glasses
raw_summary: Today, Meta, Pinacoteca di Brera and EssilorLuxottica are proud to launch “Sensing Art – Discovering Masterpieces Beyond What Meets the Eye.” This pilot aims to explore how AI glasses can make art more accessible for people who are blind or with low vision – in collaboration with the some of Italy’s leading sight loss charities – the Associazione Nazionale Subvedenti (ANS), the Unione Italiana dei Ciechi e degli Ipovedenti (UICI), and the Fondazione Istituto dei Ciechi di Milano. In one of the first projects of its kind in the world, Pinacoteca di Brera will use AI glasses developed by Meta and EssilorLuxottica to enhance the experience for blind and visually impaired people. Over one million people in Italy are blind or visually impaired, and art and culture is one of the places where accessibility can be a challenge. AI glasses give people who are blind or low vision access to transformative AI technology that can help with everyday tasks like reading text, identifying objects and accessing information about the world around them. At Meta we believe the future is for everyone, which is why we wanted to bring together this partnership. How It Works at Pinacoteca di Brera The AI glasses have been integrated with the museum’s existing Grande Brera app, which includes an audio tour guide, developed by ANS for blind and low vision visitors. The tour uses the DescriVedendo method which translates an artwork’s shapes, composition and visual details into spoken words. When a visitor stands in front of one of eight selected artworks on the itinerary as part of this pilot, they can activate artwork recognition directly from the glasses and listen to the corresponding audio description through the open-ear speakers built into the frames. The open-ear speakers help the visitor stay fully aware of their surroundings and means they can engage more naturally with people around them. The itinerary is completed by short orientation tracks between one work and the next. Visitors can also choose to utilize additional tools available through the AI glasses: Meta AI allows users to ask questions about the context and surrounding environment Be My Eyes connects visitors through the glasses with sighted volunteers and qualified operators to receive real-time support in orientation and practical task management, both during the tour. Accessibility Is Built Together The pilot project was developed through phases of testing and consultation with blind and visually impaired people. Their direct involvement helped shape both the experience and how visitors access it. “When innovation addresses real needs, it can create tangible value in people’s lives. Technology reaches its greatest potential when it succeeds in making information and daily experiences more accessible, natural, and immediate – like with our AI glasses. It is through initiatives like this—born from an ongoing dialogue with people with disabilities — that we work toward a future with more opportunities for everyone.” – Maxine Williams, VP Accessibility Meta “Making heritage accessible means creating the conditions so that everyone can build their own relationship with art. DescriVedendo has for years represented an important part of our commitment, and today we can enrich it with an additional possibility, born from the encounter between cultural expertise, technology, and people’s experience. The Pinacoteca continues to be a place of experimentation in which to explore new languages and tools capable of bringing a universal heritage closer to an ever-wider audience.” – Angelo Crespi, Director of Grande Brera How to Access the Tour The tour will be available at the Pinacoteca di Brera upon reservation, with AI glasses available Tuesday through Friday from 10:00 AM to 4:30 PM. For booking details and further information, please visit the page at this link. Battle Drones - a vibe coded RTS with audio-based multiplayer
raw_summary: My latest vibe coded game experiment is a Command & Conquer style RTS (Real Time Strategy) game called Battle Drones ( play it here ). Unlike my previous experiments , this one is actually fun to play . I'm somewhat embarrassed to admit that I got there by telling Claude to "Make it a LOT more fun". It also supports multiplayer between nearby devices using audio to synchronize game state! Here's what I've built so far, and some of the things I learned along the way. Battle Drones How I built this v1: the initial prototype v2: full sprites v3: varied terrain v4: the fun update v5: Battle Drones goes 3D v8: Archipelago v10: Goliath, and agent battles Agent battles v11: Random Maps v12: Multiplayer via sound Some thoughts Battle Drones My initial goal was to build an RTS game I could play on my phone, in the style of Command & Conquer . I have fond memories of the 1995 original (I liked Red Alert too) and wanted to recapture a little bit of the magic. After 12 major iterations (and 321 commits by coding agents, mainly Claude Code) I now have a browser-based game that works on mobile and desktop, has multiple play modes, several maps (including a random map generator) and even supports multiplayer for two devices within microphone range of each other. Here's a video demo of Battle Drones running in a desktop browser: Features so far include: 9 buildings, 7 ground vehicles, 6 aerial vehicles, 3 infantry units - all 3D models, which you can browse here Fog of war Different weapons are needed to target aerial or ground vehicles Six maps , across five biomes - temperate, desert, arctic, volcanic, tropical A random map generator Skirmish mode - red vs. blue on a rotationally symmetrical map Last Stand mode - one player holds out against as many waves of enemies as possible Area effect weapons: Barrage, EMP, Drop Pod, Sky Hammer Crate drops with bonus resources In-game music that responds to events - it gets more intense as fighting breaks out Different in-game AI personalities (Balanced, Rush, Air Swarm, Boom, Skyforce, Ironclad) AI vs. AI mode, to watch those personalities play each other The Goliath - a giant stomping mech with laser eyes and arm cannons and the ability to establish a new base Mutators that add extra rules or twists A "Daily Op" challenge Ranks and achievements ( Medals ) Agent vs. Agent mode where two LLMs can play Battle Drones against each other A multiplayer mode based on two nearby phones communicating via audio messages, an extension of my earlier experiment with Chirp Pong How I built this Battle Drones is heavily vibe coded - I've reviewed almost none of the code, and it's built in a language (TypeScript) that I've hardly used myself. I've playtested it quite a bit though, and it's been through a large number of iterations since I started the project. Here's a rough history of the project so far, including key prompts and links to transcripts. v1: the initial prototype I started out with Claude Fable 5 back in July: We are going to build a mobile friendly RTS game - command and conquer style - called Battle Drones, in which two armies of drones (both flying and ground-based) battle for territory and resources Let's start with a MVP design, ask me some questions Here's a shared transcript . I'd given Claude Code for Web an environment variable with an OpenAI API key and told it to use the OpenAI Image Generation API for assets, which got me some basic sprites. You can try v1 here - it looked like this: It's recognizable as an RTS, has building mechanics and the ability to select and direct units, and a basic AI to play against. This first version was barely a proof of concept, and it wasn't any fun to play. Claude used the Phaser 2D game framework for these early versions. I didn't even realize this until several iterations later! v2: full sprites The second version ( try v2 here ) added sprites for all of the vehicles and the "AI vs. AI" mode, so I could watch the game playing without having to directly control it myself. Claude proved reasonably competent at prompting OpenAI's image models to generate sprites. You can browse the v2 sprites in the public/assets/sprites folder. v3: varied terrain It still wasn't much fun, and the graphics were boring. It was now October, and I had upgraded to Claude Opus 5.5. I told it: Massively improve this game. Make the graphics and gameplay better (keep it mobile friendly). Render new graphics using the latest OpenAI GPT image API (lookup details) with the API key in the environment variable. Add new unit types and balance the gameplay better. Also add new buildings and better, more varied terrain. This resulted in five new maps with generated background tiles in a variety of styles, visible here . Opus also regenerated the sprites, making them much more visually appealing. You can try v3 here - it looks like this: This is starting to feel like a real game! It still wasn't very fun to play though - I found myself getting bored pretty quickly. v4: the fun update So far my Battle Drones experiment was confirming my previous belief that coding agents can build a thing that looks like a game but can't actually make something that's genuinely compelling to play. I shared this theory with someone over dinner, and then thought to myself that I should give the models a proper chance to prove me wrong. I prompted Opus 5.5 on my phone: This game isn't fun enough yet. Make it a LOT more fun. This time I was running in Ultracode mode , where Claude Code (in this case Claude Code for Web) runs "dynamic workflows", described in their docs as: A dynamic workflow is a JavaScript script that orchestrates many subagents at once. This kicked off many hours of work. I started it in the evening and didn't get a playable result back until late into the next morning. But the results were spectacular. You can try v4 here - it looks like this: I had Claude write its own release notes - here are the highlights: Every skirmish and Daily Op now opens with a choice, gives the side that's losing a way back, and pulls the armies into the middle of the map. There are also two new ways to play. Openers : pick Blitz, Industry or Air Wing before the clock starts. Call-down powers : Barrage, EMP, Drop Pod and the Sky Hammer orbital strike. Objectives and salvage : Uplink relays, supply drops and wrecks worth scrap. Feel : combat juice, adaptive music, unit voices and an announcer. Command : battle alerts, game speed, saved squads and touch placement. New modes : Last Stand survival waves and an 8-mission Ops campaign. Progression : heroes, an after-action report with awards, a career, 7 mutators and a Daily Op. Fights run longer and swing more. In 1,200 AI-vs-AI test matches on Normal, games still undecided after 25 minutes fell from 14% to 0.9%. The share of wins by a side that had been 800+ scrap behind rose from 24% to 46%. Part of the reason Claude took so long was that it ran over a thousand simulated playtest sessions, and used the results to rebalance the existing units, add new ones, and introduce new features. v5: Battle Drones goes 3D After the success of Ultracode at "Make it a LOT more fun", I decided to be more ambitious: Port this game to three.js with 3D models for all of the buildings and vehicles and landscapes That was another overnight run. I woke up to this v5 version : The new 3D models were entirely constructed by Claude in TypeScript code. v6 ( play v6 here ) added some more visual polish. v7 ( play v7 ) added robot infantry (troopers, rocket squads, snipers) and a "Condor" troop carrying aircraft. v8: Archipelago I was beginning to feel guilty at how little actual design input I had into the game - it really had been a case of me saying "make it more fun" and "add visual polish" for the past few releases. You got paid to work on tricky little logic puzzles. The trickier the puzzle, the more you got paid. But even pretty simple puzzles were worth a lot of money because regular people just couldn't do it! No, they needed us. They would give us a problem and we would solve it the way we wanted. title: How To Use Decision Models for Evals
raw_summary: Decision models have exploded onto the scene recently, starting with TypeSafe’s Jev, followed by Perplexity’s Decider, Liquid’s d1, Cloudflare’s Clef, and OpenAI’s Decisions API 1 . These models promise fast, inexpensive classification. Decision models are an appealing low-cost alternative to LLM judges 2 for automated evals. But whether they’re the right choice depends on the cost, performance, and latency requirements of your use case. We’ve also noticed people using the default decision threshold of 0.50 without checking whether it works well for their task. This can leave a lot of performance on the table. In this post, we’ll start by showing how to tune thresholds to get the best results from decision models. With those thresholds tuned, we’ll compare cost and performance to help you assess which model fits your use case. Finally, we’ll explore how to interpret model scores when deciding whether to act, and how calibration can make them more useful as confidence estimates. What we tested We used 100 traces, or logs of conversations and actions, from an apartment leasing agent. The task is to identify traces containing an error, such as a failed booking or a missed handoff to a human. 3 We used the same dataset and broad failure-finding task in our prior post on automated evals . Here, each decision model returns a failure probability for each trace. We tested Jev 1.13, Perplexity Decider 1.1 27B, Liquid d1 and d1-ultra, Cloudflare Clef Flash, and OpenAI Decisions (GPT-6 Luna) 1 . Each model received the same evaluation criteria. The appendix shows the prompt and the structured version used for Jev. We compare models on two dimensions: Performance: We compare each model’s predictions with traces that people have reviewed and labeled as passing or failing. This measures how well the model catches failures while avoiding false alarms. Cost: We calculate API cost from token usage and the provider’s prices. 4 For brevity, we leave latency aside because it depends on factors outside this experiment’s control. 5 Understanding decision thresholds We assign each trace one of two labels, pass or fail. This is a binary pass/fail eval , which we recommend because it encourages clear criteria and is easier to align with human preferences. Each decision model returns a score from 0 to 1 that estimates how likely a trace is to contain a failure. The APIs turn this score into a decision using a default decision threshold of 0.50 . Traces with scores at or above the threshold are flagged as failures. Using this default without checking it against your data can give you subpar results. For example, a model could assign every failure a score of 0.40 and every passing trace a score of 0.10. Even though this model classifies traces perfectly at a threshold of 0.30, the default threshold of 0.50 would catch nothing. In practice, scores for failures and passing traces will overlap. Lowering the threshold catches more failures but can also raise more false alarms. Choosing a threshold means balancing: Precision: The share of flagged traces that contain a known failure. Recall: The share of known failures that the model catches. The right tradeoff depends on your business goals. For example, criminal trials set a high bar for conviction to avoid convicting innocent people, emphasizing precision. Cancer screening may emphasize recall, accepting more false alarms to miss fewer cases. 6 For this comparison, we’ll give precision and recall equal weight using the F1 score , their harmonic mean. F1 ranges from 0 to 1, and higher is better. The curves below show how each model scores failures (orange) and passing traces (blue). Taller parts of a curve mean more scores from that class fall in that range. Scores at or above the dashed threshold line are flagged. Use the toggle to compare 0.50 with Optimized for best F1 , which chooses a threshold for each model. 7 OpenAI separates the two classes best on this task, which is also reflected in its higher F1 score. It’s also important not to blindly maximize F1 without thinking about your minimum requirements for the classifier to be useful. For example, if this classifier is used for an automated alerting system, I would want a minimum of 80% on both precision and recall so that I’m minimizing false alarms while catching a sufficient number of failures. The chart below shows how precision and recall change at different thresholds. 8 The shaded region marks where both reach at least 80%. Perplexity, Liquid d1-ultra, and OpenAI Decisions meet our requirements, but we still need to choose a decision threshold within the shaded region for each model. In the next section, we’ll discuss how to tune those thresholds. Tuning the decision threshold For this example, we’ll optimize F1. For our candidates, we’ll restrict tuning to thresholds that meet both 80% minimums on the training data whenever possible. We leave the other models unconstrained to illustrate the effect of tuning. 9 With labeled traces and saved model scores, you can ask a coding agent to tune the thresholds. Below is an example prompt you can modify for your use case: Using my saved model scores and binary labels (1 means failure), tune a decision threshold to maximize F1 while requiring at least 80% precision and 80% recall. Use stratified five-fold cross-validation, choosing thresholds on the training examples and measuring performance on the remaining examples. If comparing models, use the same splits for each. Only select thresholds that meet both minimums on the training examples. If none qualifies, report that rather than relaxing either requirement. Report validation precision, recall, and F1, along with any splits where no threshold qualified or validation performance fell below my minimums. Compare with the default threshold of 0.50. Reuse the saved scores without making new model calls. Here’s how tuning for F1 changed each model’s performance. We group the three candidates from the precision-recall chart together and show the other models in gray to illustrate how much tuning can help. Our candidate models gained less from F1 tuning than Liquid d1 and Clef Flash, which fell below our minimums. However, even a small shift in precision and recall can affect business costs or the user experience, so choose the tradeoff deliberately. In practice, it’s unlikely that precision and recall are equally important (as we assumed in this post with F1). For example, the F-beta score lets you give precision more weight with beta below 1, or recall more weight with beta above 1. Optimizing a different metric could lead to different thresholds and results. Performance versus cost The chart below compares each model’s F1 (after tuning) against cost, focused on our remaining candidates: The dashed line shows the Pareto frontier among our remaining candidates. For any given F1 score, it identifies the cheapest candidate that meets or exceeds that score. title: Training AIs to Solve CAPTCHAs
raw_summary: Interesting research : Abstract : Vision-language models (VLMs) can solve visual CAPTCHAs without task-specific training, but the agents built on them approach every challenge from scratch. For such an agent, the hundredth instance of a familiar puzzle costs as much time and compute as the first. Specialized detectors invert the trade-off, answering in milliseconds but only for categories they were trained on. Neither improves with exposure. We study what changes when a solver improves with use. Our system pairs a fine-tuned YOLOv8 detector with an open-weight VLM behind a confidence-based router, and runs entirely from screenshots and operating-system input events, with no browser automation or DOM access. It reaches 85.4% overall and 84.2% macro accuracy across 16 classes, exceeding either component alone. Every answer VLM produces also serves as a training label, so the detector absorbs categories it was never trained for, typically after one or two encounters and without human annotation. The same loop also repairs it. A CAPTCHA operator can perturb images against the publicly released detector and drive its accuracy to 0%, but the perturbations leave VLM untouched, and its labels let the detector recover. Under a year-long simulated arms race in which the CAPTCHA operator re-crafts its perturbations each month, the solver recovers every round, and a cheap ~70%-accurate open-weight teacher hardens it as effectively as a perfect oracle. Visual CAPTCHA defenses that assume a failing bot stays failing therefore understate how quickly an adaptive solver returns...

title: Search and Increasing Returns, or, No One Makes You Push to Github
raw_summary: Attention conservation notice : An economistic argument that computer networks are nigh-doomed to effective centralization, by someone who is neither an economist nor a computer scientist. Arcane, speculative, and not actionable even if correct. You would be better off spending your time reading a book . Drafted in 2018, and deliberately not much updated. Posted now because I found myself re-using the joke of the subtitle in an e-mail. Twitter is awful for many reasons , but not the least of them is the way it makes its users feel forced to keep using it. ( One such complaint among many .) Early visions of how it could contribute to a beneficient or at least harmless ecosystem, such Steven Berlin Johnson's (*), presumed that it would be much less sticky , a more old-fashioned website people could leave. Now, more recently Johnson has written a spectacularly wrong-headed piece hailing blockchain as a blow for re-decentralizing the Web. Of course, the primary working example of a block chain is Bitcoin, which is heavily centralized in holdings, in processing power, and in exchanges. And there are economies-of-scale reasons to expect this would be true of anything using either proof of work or proof of stake. But suppose the problem with Bitcoin is just that it's not got a very compelling use: imagine if keeping your car idling 24/7 produced solved Sudokus you could trade for heroin --- @Theophite, 16 August 2018 and that nobody has a use for blockchains , not really. Git repositories, on the other hand, are the part of the blockchain idea that's actually good for something: a way of tracking changes, with many authors, where it is very, very hard to go back and alter history without being caught. And git repositories are things that are in-principle easy to copy and move around, and could be hosted on any machine running HTTP (or, heck, FTP). So why does Github exist , let alone hold the position it does? The answer, I think, comes in two parts. The first is that focal points are subject to increasing returns via network effects. The second is that search engines create and/or amplify focal points . Put these two together, and you get a very strong tendency for any particular line of activity --- be it trading solved sudokus for heroin or open-source software development --- to concentrate in just one, or at most a few, online locations. Incidentally: This doesn't necessarily lock in first-mover advantage, because other forces can overcome this (revulsion, technical superiority), but it does mean that it will be very hard to avoid having at most a few dominant locations at any one time. It also means that the transitions between dominant locations will be brief . If we really wanted to re-decentralize, we'd have to (1) get rid of focal points, or (2) get rid of search engines as we've known them, or (3) somehow make search conduct users to a distributed, decentralized focal "non-point" (focal blob? focal rhizome?). I therefore strongly suspect we are not going to re-decentralize. But then I didn't expect the Web would centralize as much as it has, despite having literally learned my Brian Arthur and Paul David at my father's knee, so what do I know? *: To be clear, I have been a fan of Johnson's books since Interface Culture and Emergence . I am picking on two of his essays, but that's because I think he is too ready to find encouraging signs for a certain vision of how the Internet could transform the world for the better. To be clear, I share the vision, but now hold out little hope for it . (Tweakage, 2 June 2026: Small changes in the last paragraph, avoid re-using the word "point" so much.) A true Burkean conservative in America should work for the preservation and development of the institutions bequeathed us by our wise and heroic ancestors, serving us for half a century, a century, or more: the welfare state; the regulatory agencies; international organizations and treaties; the military-industrial complex; academia; affirmative action; Hollywood and the rest of corporate popular culture. Going "something something ergodicity mumble mumble sampling reveals a process grumble grumble shut up and calculate" makes this only a little less weird to me. A good philosophy of probability should explain why all applied Bayesian statistics relies on Monte Carlo, the most frequentist method imaginable. title: Using Kedro to build reusable reflection systems for enterprise AI agents
raw_summary: Modular pipelines, data contracts, and approval gates for agent improvement In a recent post on this channel, “ Smart contracts for AI agents ”, we described embedding governance directly into each agent through a machine-readable manifest and a runtime sidecar proxy. We noted how it addresses four scaling problems: framework-selection paralysis, compliance drift, reactive validation, and vendor lock-in. The smart contract defines what the agent is, and the sidecar enforces it. However, an agent may operate fully within its declared boundaries while still producing weak outputs, for example, by falling short of quality targets, or drifting in patterns that emerge only across dozens of runs and several campaigns. The smart contracts approach can tell you that your agent used an unapproved model or accessed restricted data, but it cannot tell you about the quality of the emails your sales agent writes on your behalf. Are they any good? Are they improving over time? What is missing is a way to accumulate learning at scale. That requires another layer, positioned above enforcement, which converts production traces into organizational knowledge. This article describes what a learning layer looks like and how to build it as shared infrastructure rather than a one-off feature bolted onto each agent. Why learning gets trapped in silos Enterprises running multiple agents tend to converge on the same organizational problem. One team builds an evaluation rubric for a sales outreach agent. Another adds observability to a marketing campaign agent. A third writes its own reflection workflow for customer care. Each team reinvents the same cycle: generate output → score it → detect what went wrong → propose a fix → review and approve it → apply it. Their fixes stay local to their agents. A regression test written for the B2B sales agent never reaches the consumer marketing agent. A quality pattern that recurs in both sales and marketing sits in two separate dashboards. There isn’t a portfolio-level view of which agents are improving, which are degrading, and what failure modes they share. The underlying issue is that improvement is treated as a feature of individual agents, not as a common layer that every team and campaign can reuse. This builds on an idea we introduced in our original article, “ Agentic AI Mesh ”, which described feedback loops where “agents configured to critique outputs of other agents… can be used to signal positive and negative performance, triggering the automated development of configuration variations that can be tested and scored.” What that article didn’t specify was the shared infrastructure, such as approval gates, versioning, and cross-campaign visibility, that is needed to operationalize that loop, and that is what we cover here. A shared reflection infrastructure Agentic reflection is the process by which a system designed to evaluate agent performance reviews an agent’s outputs against predefined quality criteria, identifies errors or reasoning gaps, and proposes improvements. The learning part happens when improvements are approved, captured, and reused so that mistakes are not repeated. Building this as shared infrastructure requires the same three structural properties that make the smart contract architecture work. Declarative: Evaluation logic, reflection prompts, approval rules, and improvement steps are written down and versioned rather than embedded in ad hoc scripts that only the team that wrote them can access. Modular: Generation, evaluation, signal detection, reflection, and application are separate stages that can change independently. A team that wants to swap the evaluation model does not need to touch the generation pipeline. Reusable: The loop, the deterministic checks, and the audit trail are common to every agent, and the scouts flag when the same type of failure recurs in more than one agent. Approved changes are versioned and visible across the portfolio, so a fix found by one team can be reviewed and adopted by another. A worked example using Kedro We built an example of this approach using Kedro , an open-source Python framework, which offers a modular pipeline structure and explicit data contracts to provide a set of building blocks. Using Kedro to take care of the surrounding orchestration enabled us to focus on the reflection and learning workflow. To show how this pattern works in practice, we built an example that applies the same reflection and learning workflow across three business functions (B2B sales, consumer marketing, and customer care) in a telecommunications company. The improvement lifecycle Each function uses different data sources, prompts, and evaluation criteria. The improvement lifecycle is identical for all three: Generate: run the AI workflow and capture outputs. Evaluate: score outputs against quality criteria using a versioned rubric and an LLM judge. Identify signals and patterns: detect recurring issues across runs, such as tone drift, hallucinations, missing required content, or score regressions. Reflect: generate targeted recommendations such as prompt updates, skill edits, or evaluation logic changes. Review and approve: a human reviewer inspects the proposed changes and approves or rejects them through an explicit approval gate. Nothing goes live without it. Apply: version and commit the approved changes, and record each one in an audit log. A screen from the Kedro reflection agent example In the example, the generate, evaluate, detect, reflect, and apply stages are separate pipelines, with review and approval acting as an approval gate. The pipelines, deterministic checks, and approval gate are shared, while the prompts, style guides, rubrics, and LLM judge dimensions change by use case. Reflection also proposes new regression cases derived from the failures it found. Once approved, they are committed to that agent’s evaluation dataset (alongside any approved changes to the prompt, skills, or other configurable components) then every change is recorded in a single audit log. The signal moves between agents. When the same type of failure recurs in more than one agent, the scouts record it in a shared signal index and flag it as a cross-unit pattern, rather than leaving it as two unrelated findings in two isolated dashboards. A reviewer can then decide whether a fix belongs to one agent or should be adopted by others. Reflection maps onto a Shape-Control-Operate (SCO) lifecycle. Prompts and evaluation criteria are defined in the Shape phase, and evaluation scoring runs in the Control phase. The evidence gathered while agents Operate then feeds approved changes back into the Shape-phase artifacts, which closes the loop. How the evaluation step works Evaluation uses a fixed set of benchmark cases but does not rely on a single correct or “golden” output. Each case, stored in Langfuse and cached locally, pairs a scenario — customer, product, and case ID — with a rubric defining required and forbidden content, expected call to action, tone, and other agent-specific criteria. For each case, the generation pipeline produces an output, which is then scored in two ways: Deterministic checks validate objective requirements such as subject presence, body length, CTA presence, and fabricated SKU-like tokens. An LLM judge evaluates qualitative dimensions such as writing quality, personalization, and groundedness. These dimensions can vary by agent (for example, empathy or compliance). A case passes when the average score across all scorers meets the configured threshold. Results are captured at both case and aggregate levels and logged to Langfuse, enabling teams to compare runs after prompt changes, inspect traces, and feed the findings back into the reflection loop. The business impact of the solution is cumulative. Every run, signal, and approved change is recorded, to extend the learning history of each reflection. title: Building production-ready GraphRAG systems with Kedro
raw_summary: A demo project to manage the graph, vector index, and relational store Standard Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) works well for factual lookup. For example, if you use semantic similarity to retrieve a document, you’ll usually find the correct passage. However, it struggles when the lookup requires reasoning across relationships, say if the answer depends on facts that are distributed across records that share little lexical or semantic similarity with each other. As an illustration for healthcare, a search might want to discover the risk of a particular medication to patients with a certain condition. A typical query might be: “ For a chronic kidney disease patient, which medication may not be safe and interact with their poor kidney function? ” A dense retriever might return the passages whose embeddings sit the closest to the query vector, like a chunk about chronic kidney disease and another about drugs with contraindications for renal patients. But to respond to this question as accurately as possible, we’d have to gather information from separate records, like a diagnosis note, a lab report, or a drug prescription. None of these directly references the others, and there is no structure that encodes the intersection of all of these pieces of data. GraphRAG addresses this by pairing semantic search with a knowledge graph that represents the structure explicitly: entities such as conditions, medications, and test results become nodes, and the relationships between them become edges. Before passing context to the language model, the system traverses the relationships connected to the retrieved entities so the model can reason across linked nodes rather than treating each document in isolation. In this article, we describe how we used Kedro to build a demo of a simple reference implementation. The basics In our example, the GraphRAG system maintains three representations of the same underlying data, which need to stay consistent with each other as source data changes. The representations are: a knowledge graph for relationship traversal a vector index for semantic retrieval a relational store for aggregate statistics. Data engineering matters as much as retrieval because of the need for consistency. Inconsistent data arises, for example, when data teams use a collection of scripts, run in undocumented order, with no guarantee that the graph, the vector index, and the analytics store are produced from the same source run. When the knowledge graph becomes stale relative to the embeddings, the retrieval and graph traversal return contradictory context. As a result, the model resolves the inconsistency silently, and may resolve it incorrectly. A data engineering pipeline feeds all three data stores. Incremental updates compound the challenge. Rebuilding the full graph each time new records arrive is impractical at production scale. A production system needs targeted, merge-capable updates that leave unchanged nodes and edges untouched while incorporating new information: a classic data engineering pipeline problem. An example pipeline Using Kedro , we built a five-stage pipeline demo over a synthetic healthcare dataset of 55,500 patient records covering conditions, medications, insurers, admission types, diagnostic results, and demographics. The full source is on the Kedro Academy GitHub repository . While this example is based on healthcare data, none of this structure is specific to healthcare, and the example is deliberately simple to keep it self-contained and easy to run. The entity extraction, graph building patterns, and incremental merge logic apply to any domain with typed entities and relationships. A graph built from a synthetic healthcare dataset of 55,500 patient records in this simple and self-contained example. The pipeline stages are as follows: Clean and summarize: The first stage normalizes raw records, removes duplicates, and computes summary statistics per entity. We used patient counts per condition, average billing amounts per admission type, and result distributions across demographic groups. This stage stores them in SQLite and reuses them as retrieval context in later stages. Build the knowledge graph: The second stage extracts entities and typed relationships. Nodes represent conditions , medications , insurers , admission types , test results , and blood types . Edges carry a relationship label (TREATED_WITH, COVERED_BY, ADMITTED_AS, SHOWS_RESULT, ASSOCIATED_WITH) and a weight recording how frequently each relationship appears in the data. The stage produces a NetworkX JSON graph with 30 nodes and 120 weighted edges, and an interactive D3.js visualization of the entity network. Incrementally update the graph: Rather than rebuilding from scratch on each data refresh, the next stage merges new records into the existing graph using create-or-update semantics. It adds new entities, increments edge weights for existing relationships, and leaves unchanged portions untouched. In this demo, each run of the stage merges a fixed batch of 5,000 records rather than the full corpus, and it updates only the knowledge graph. We designed it to model a real production constraint: while rebuilding a relatively small graph like this is cheap and resolves in a few seconds, a production-sized knowledge graph based on a larger, more complex set of data would take much longer. Generate vector embeddings: For each entity, the next stage generates a natural-language summary of its characteristics and connections, then embeds those summaries using OpenAI’s text-embedding-3-small model . This stage stores the embeddings in ChromaDB for semantic similarity search at query time. Answer questions: The final stage runs an AI agent backed by GPT-4o. When a query arrives, the agent embeds it and queries ChromaDB for the most similar entity summaries. Starting from those results, it traverses one hop across the knowledge graph to collect neighboring entities and the relationships between them. That combined context (semantic matches plus explicit graph structure) goes to the model. Standard RAG asks, “ What is most similar to this query? ” This stage adds, “ What else is connected to those results? ” This is a hybrid GraphRAG pattern: vector retrieval followed by graph traversal. All five stages write to three different backends, and Kedro’s Data Catalog manages loading and saving for all of them from a single configuration file. Every dataset (the NetworkX graph, the ChromaDB collection, the SQLite statistics table, the LangChain prompt template) is declared in catalog.yml so there is one place to see where each input and output lives and there are no separate scripts to reconcile manually. A full default run builds all three stores from the same source data. The incremental update refreshes only the knowledge graph; keeping the vector index and statistics in step with it would require extending their pipelines in the same way. Each stage is an independent Kedro pipeline with explicit inputs and outputs. The graph construction logic, the embedding model, and the retrieval strategy sit in separate modules. Swapping the embedding model requires changing one node and its catalog entry, while the graph and statistics stages are unaffected. Kedro-Viz renders the full data lineage across all five stages, and a published Kedro-Viz build can be viewed without any installation on the viewer’s side. This approach also means it is possible to treat generative AI components as first-class Data Catalog entries, rather than scripts or loose objects spread around the project. It makes them easier to manage and keep track of, and they can be used as input or output for nodes like any other entry. Through the use of Kedro, generative AI datasets receive easy credentials management and follow the same load/save contract as other Kedro datasets. The graph_update pipeline is excluded from the default run and must be invoked explicitly. It writes to the same catalog entry …

title: What changes when your design system can talk to an AI?
raw_summary: Rebuilding a UI with QuantumBlack Design System, Claude Code, and the Figma MCP In our recent blog post, “ When everyone can build, design is the differentiator ”, we introduced QuantumBlack Design System (QBDS). We made the argument that an AI-native design system is more than a component library and its purpose is as an infrastructure that lets agentic developers make fewer guesses. The article described the system and our philosophy. Over the past few weeks, we have re-platformed the entire UI of one of our products onto QBDS, one that previously had a production dashboard built on an older shadcn layout that predated QBDS. In numbers, it runs to 21 pages, 13 modals, 40 UI primitives and somewhere around 96 supporting components. A refactor of this size used to mean months of redlines and handoff documents. We’ll describe what we discovered from using QBDS, both from the engineering side and the design side. In this post we’ll describe what happened when we put QuantumBlack Design System to work. The setup We used a small stack since QBDS supplies the components, the tokens, and the agent guidance described in the earlier QBDS article linked above. We used Figma to hold the target designs, and Claude Code for the implementation, connected through the Figma MCP server . We crafted an internal QuantumBlack front-end developer skill to package QBDS guidance in the form an agent can act on. That skill lives on Brix , our inner source platform for sharing artefacts. The workflow Our front-end engineer runs a page migration roughly as shown in the diagram. A typical page migration workflow for a FE engineer. Spin up the app locally with hot reloading. Give Claude the context: the PR, a screenshot of the current screen, the target Figma node, and the skill. Instruct the agent to ask when something isn’t trivial. Review every change as it lands live, through hot reload. Run unit tests and lint (Claude fixes most failures itself), then draft the PR, run CI/CD, and run manual Playwright E2E tests on a local minikube. Use a review bot initially, then have a human review the result before the merge. Step 3 is more than a throwaway. For example, when Claude migrated the Secrets page, the Figma node left two questions open: how row actions should render, and what to do with two modals the design didn’t cover. Rather than making a guess, it set out the gaps, weighed each option against the pages we’d already migrated, and asked for clarification. We answered in two lines and it then completed the build. The agent noticed that one option “diverges from other migrated tables,” which means that the agent had to know what the other migrated tables do. This knowledge came about because QBDS encodes patterns and relationships, not only components, which is the benefit of using QBDS over a plain component library. In time terms: a simple table page with an existing sibling pattern took 10 to 15 minutes end to end, with tests and build included. A complex screen from scratch took 4 to 5 hours. If we had worked on this migration by hand, both would have taken days. What the design side measures Our designer’s comparison is against a similar product we shipped last year, before QBDS or any of this tooling existed: First-pass fidelity to Figma: around 20 percent previously, 70–80 percent now we’re using this workflow. Review rounds per screen: four or more previously, and the result often still wasn’t right. One or two now, and the result is correct. Component reuse: we now reuse about 90 percent from stock QBDS components. The other 10 percent is custom, but assembled from QBDS micro-elements as a starting point. QA and handoff: three-plus hours per screen previously, much of it spent writing Figma documentation so engineering could interpret intent, and we sometimes also needed a meeting to decide. With the new workflow we now need twenty minutes to an hour. This is a key result because previously handoff was a translation problem from human to agent. Now we can use QBDS, the system documentation is already readable by the agent, so most of the laborious translation work is now unnecessary. A typical page before and after refactoring. The broader role of a designer It’s difficult to capture this in a metric, but ultimately, designers on our team don’t live in Figma any more. We’ve expanded our AI skills and ways of working, so depending on what we’re trying to solve, that might mean working in Figma, Cursor, or Claude Code, or moving between them. The choice of tool becomes more intentional, based on what each part of the problem actually needs. With QBDS in the codebase, we can work against the same system the product actually ships with. Through the Figma MCP, our QBDS skills and Code Connect, we carry context between design and code instead of recreating it at every step. When something is easier to explore visually, we work in Figma. When we want to experience it in the real product, we move into code. That changes the traditional design-to-development handoff. With AI, designers can take an idea further, from exploring the experience to composing it with real components, implementing the front end, and experiencing the design in the actual product. AI doesn’t get everything right by default, and the quality of the result depends heavily on the context and tools we give the agent. title: Solving the data lineage problem that’s holding enterprise AI back
raw_summary: AI4Data by QuantumBlack, AI by McKinsey Data estates rarely become complex by design. They grow through acquisitions, new platforms, local workarounds, and repeated efforts to connect, consolidate, or retire legacy systems. While such changes are often necessary, each one opens the door to duplicated data, undocumented transformation logic, and inconsistent definitions. Even when individual datasets are high quality, teams may no longer know the lineage of data, that is, where a value originated, nor how it changed between systems, or which version should be treated as authoritative. Most enterprises still build lineage manually. Teams piece it together from institutional knowledge, often relying on the few subject-matter experts who remember how a dataset was assembled. Because documentation is frequently incomplete and becomes outdated quickly, analysts spend disproportionate time finding and validating data. Projects are stalled, data is duplicated rather than reused, and different teams repeatedly investigate the same relationships. This article describes how to accelerate the creation of trusted, end-to-end data lineage. Everyone has a reason to invest in data lineage Until recently, the firms that invested seriously in lineage were regulated firms such as banks, insurers, and healthcare organizations, and they did it because their regulators required it. Since 2020, those sectors have paid more than $1.4B in finalized regulatory penalties, often due to deficient monitoring and reporting frameworks, and failures to meet standards such as BCBS 239. The response was to throw people at the problem. In complex data environments, tracing the path of a single element from report to data source can take weeks, largely because the relevant knowledge is scattered across ETL tools, data catalogs, and the memories of individual employees. Firms outside regulated industries looked at that cost and reasonably decided they could live without lineage. Unresolved lineage stands in the way of both regulatory compliance and the cost reductions that come from a modernized legacy data estate. The scale of the underlying spend explains why: procuring data sources and maintaining data governance can account for roughly a fifth of total IT spend at a large institution, with more than half of that going toward data controls and manual governance activity alone. By improving lineage and reducing the effort required to trace, validate, and remediate data issues, organizations may be able to realize an estimated $30–100M in cost savings. The harder-won benefit is trust: executives get a defensible reason to believe the dashboards they already use and the agents they are being asked to rely on. An AI agent asked to answer a question from enterprise data has to know which source is authoritative and what happened to a value between systems. Without lineage, the agent either guesses or the organization refuses to trust what it returns. Every sector deploying agents now needs lineage across a far wider slice of the estate than a regulatory report ever covered. Manual lineage can’t keep pace Most lineage tools available today are point solutions which trace how data moves within a single system, leaving organizations struggling when faced with more complex enterprise estates. It’s not unusual for an estate to comprise dozens of systems, built years or decades apart, on a wide variety of legacy platforms and programming languages with undocumented logic. This helps explain why up to three-quarters of organizations still rely on manual work to trace the lineage of their most critical data, an incredibly slow and expensive process. Manually tracing a single data element end-to-end across legacy and cloud systems typically has a direct cost of one to three million dollars. Recent advancements in AI that have emerged over the past year enable the interpretation of code and metadata alongside the raw data itself, detecting connections across any environment or platform. These automated tools can complement the lineage tools organizations already have, closing gaps between them and accelerating those tasks that used to require an army of analysts. This rest of this article explains how AI for data lineage (AI4DL) from QuantumBlack, AI by McKinsey, addresses a shared bottleneck by accelerating lineage creation, to give organizations a clearer view of where data comes from and how it changes across systems. AI4DL accelerates one core task across four common use cases AI4DL is an accelerator that combines AI-based detection methods with human validation to identify complete, end-to-end lineage across whatever mix of systems and technologies a client happens to run. It’s designed to capture lineage faster and more completely, engendering greater trust than any manual approach can. AI4DL is an accelerator for creating lineage output that is reusable, and provides many different types of business value, depending on the use case. Regulatory traceability: AI4DL gives compliance teams real and up-to-date visibility into how data flows, transforms, and depends on other data across systems. Improved data and business understanding: AI4DL exposes origins, dependencies, transformations, and consumption patterns across the data estate. Migration readiness: AI4DL accelerates the mapping between legacy and modern data models, cutting the effort required for platform and code migrations. AI and analytics implementation: AI4DL gives AI agents validated context for finding, interpreting, and using enterprise data. Together, these benefits build a level of trust that enables a regulator, a migration lead, and a data engineering team to point to the same underlying lineage graph and trust it for their own purposes, rather than maintaining separate, often incomplete versions of the truth. Solving data lineage can unlock gen Al and agentic workflows in organizations. Productivity is the shared economic benefit across all four use cases. By reducing manual lineage documentation, investigation, and validation, AI4DL frees data, engineering, governance, and subject-matter experts to focus on higher-value work. AI detection and human checks AI4DL works by running various detection methods in parallel, each tuned to a different signal in the data estate: LLM-based metadata inference reads data catalogs (table and column names, descriptions, constraints, tags, owners) to infer likely lineage. LLM-based code review parses ETL and ELT code, from SQL to PySpark to DAGs, to derive column-level lineage and summarize what each transformation actually does. Statistical attribute matching suggests column similarities between different datasets using data profiling and distribution similarity. The same approach used for a single COBOL program, for example, can be scaled to two thousand or more, with the same degree of accuracy and trust. Whatever combination of methods applies, the results are never taken at face value. The tool flags low confidence decisions and human experts review the resulting lineage graphs, so that they flag inconsistencies before anything is treated as fact. This human check is what allows AI4DL’s output to be treated as audit-grade rather than merely directional, a critical distinction in regulated industries. The results Example: A major Latin American bank pursuing an AI-first strategy was being held back by data quality issues with ten years of real-time credit card and investment data, more than 34 billion rows spread across 2,000-plus COBOL programs and 50-plus DB2 tables. title: The Alignment Problem: Computer Science Meets Analytic Philosophy
raw_summary: TLDR: I explain what the technical AI alignment problem is and what its core difficulties are, in my view. This is a perspective that draws simultaneously on classical traditions in theoretical computer science / machine learning theory, ideas from analytic philosophy, and views that originated in the Machine Intelligence Research Institute / LessWrong. Minimal Viable Safety The Task The problem of making AI safe is underspecified if we haven't decided what the AI is supposed to do . For example, we can run any AI inside a homomorphic encryption box and never decrypt the output. This is probably perfectly safe [1] , but also perfectly useless. We can decide on an arbitrary task such as "construct Lean proofs for given mathematical theorems" and declare victory once we have safe AI that does it with superhuman skill [2] . However, that wouldn't address the danger. First, there would be incentives to use AI for tasks to which our solution doesn't apply. Second, even if we had precise safety guidelines for any task that anyone cares about, there would always be actors that ignore the guidelines, and we probably need Artificial Superintelligence (ASI) to reliably stop them. If anyone, anywhere, creates an unrestricted unaligned ASI agent (more details about the word "agent" later), without an aligned ASI agent already in place to counteract it, then a catastrophic outcome is highly likely. I will not go into the reasons here: this has been discussed elsewhere at length, see for example the books I cited in the preface. Therefore, this event is something which we must never allow to happen. This is the main threat model that I set out to address. Imagine a world in which anyone with sufficient resources has the ability to destroy the world. Like today, many will foolishly believe that instead of destroying the world, this act will bring them power and glory. Moreover, as computing hardware improves and new algorithms are developed, the amount of resources for this act will go down from year to year. Even assuming best-case regulation and international agreements, how long until someone does it? Can mere humans build a society which will be foolproof against such a risk over the course of generations? Resilient to any political upheavals that might come, and undoubtedly will? I find it vanishingly unlikely. Eventually we will need the help of ASI itself. Therefore, the minimal task that safe AI must be able to solve is "create a reliable global defense system against dangerous AI" (in the following, GDS). The Problem Consider the consequences of this task for the capabilities that the AI needs to have. It needs to reason about the entire planet [3] . It needs to reason about all aspects of the problem, including scientific, technological, social, political and moral [4] . It needs to have preferences about the state of the world. It needs to make long-term plans (guided by these preferences) that would play out decades, if not centuries, into the future. And it needs to do all that on a superhuman level. In this light, here is how I (informally) define the "technical AI alignment problem". The problem is designing an AI system that can bring scalable (and ultimately superhuman) capability to bear on problems that require multi-domain reasoning and open-world long-term planning with far-reaching consequences, all the while staying aligned with the intentions and preferences of its human users. The Methodology What kind of methodology is appropriate for this problem? In the past, I argued that it requires emphasis on deep theoretical understanding, rather than the incremental trial-and-error approach that is employed in the AI industry today. I won't rehash the entire debate here, but let me recap the core argument. The nature of the incremental approach is as follows: we build a system, then we find problems [5] , then we make changes to fix these problems to the extent necessary for commercial viability in the current legal environment. We make some improvements; new problems arise (sometimes because of the improvements, sometimes because of new applications or other reasons); rinse and repeat. This approach utterly fails if the "problems" result in AI takeover and possibly human extinction: there is nobody left to fix them. In order for the incremental approach to succeed in preventing catastrophe, we need to reach a point where no new substantial problems arise, even inside the lab (before the system is deployed). Moreover, we need to reach this point before AI capabilities are sufficient for AI to escape our control. There are few reasons to expect such a miracle. On the contrary, sufficiently advanced AI might understand that it is in its interest to "lie low" (i.e. avoid visibly misaligned behaviors) until its capabilities cross the relevant threshold, such that the problems will only become apparent too late. In contrast, the sane approach is creating the theoretical tools necessary to predict and prevent the problems before they are empirically observed. These tools need to remain applicable as AI capabilities rise substantially beyond human, for whatever algorithms, architectures and training protocols are used to achieve these capabilities. Moreover, these tools need to be extremely reliable for us to rationally trust them with the safety of our entire species. The Challenge While the theory of machine learning and AI is an established field with ample literature, its current state falls well short of the challenge. The core difficulties can be summarized as follows: Hypercomplexity: It is infeasible to explicitly specify user preferences outside narrow domains, and narrow domains are not enough. Nor is it possible to explicitly specify a satisfactory model of the world. Therefore, learning is necessary. Alignment Grounding: When trying to learn user preferences, it is unclear what loss function or success metric can work outside narrow domains. Nor is it clear how to specify such a metric for metaphysically realist world-models, which are necessary here. Nor is it even clear what type of mathematical objects can formally describe these concepts. Alignment Convergence: Even given a success metric, it is unclear how to produce guarantees for optimizing this metric, given the ubiquity of irreversible mistakes and the lack of a theory of generalization for powerful learners. Side-Channel Resilience: The usual abstraction of "learner" is insufficient here, since we need to ensure the safety of internal computations rather than just external outputs. In the following, we will examine these difficulties one by one. But first, let's discuss what we need to accomplish. Alignment is Holistic Per the discussion above, our interest lies in AI systems that have open-world preferences and make effective plans to advance these preferences. In particular, making such plans requires learning a sophisticated model of the world and updating the model and the plan as additional information becomes available. We will call such a system an AI agent . In order for an AI agent to be aligned, it needs to have aligned preferences and beliefs , and follow an aligned decision-making algorithm on the basis of these preferences and beliefs. While discussions about AI alignment often focus on the "preferences" part, beliefs and decisions are equally important. (Although it's true that preferences bring extra wrinkles into the problem as they are, arguably, the most "subjective" component in the trio.) In this context "aligned" preferences typically means preferences very similar to those of the user(s) [6] , at least within some domain that we are somehow constrained to inhabit. On the other hand, "aligned" beliefs doesn't mean beliefs that are similar to those of the user: on the contrary, we expect the AI agent to acquire more accurate beliefs. title: Deconfusing Corrigibility
raw_summary: Many thanks to Abram Demski for materially and intellectually supporting this research. Thanks also to Brian Berns, Roman Malov, Gurkenglas, and Lorxus for valuable conversations. Introduction Despite the central place of corrigibility to theoretical AI alignment, it seems like no one can really agree about what is . Much of this confusion is due to the fact that almost every definition of corrigibility proposed thus far is deficient in one way or another. In particular, the most prevalent existing accounts of corrigibility are over-epistemicized (modeling corrigibility as arising purely from uncertainty about the AI's goal, which gives rise to issues like the problem of fully updated deference) or evaluatively-thickened (making the AI's normative priorities instrumental to its corrigibility as a result of forcing corrigibility to be a single unified goal.) Here, my intention is to clear up some of these confusions and present a new picture of corrigibility that builds on these existing accounts to specify a goal that is more congruous with the original 2015 desiderata , and admits the kind of formal safety guarantees we need the concept to entail. I argue that the fundamental concept underlying corrigibility is respect for authority , using the analogy of a healthcare proxy's relationship to a patient as an intuitive guide. Defining the authority of humanity by designating its reserved powers , we can specify a goal that first and foremost restrains the agent from overstepping or interfering with this reserved human authority. Subject to this restraint, the agent then pursues the second component of its goal: acting on the principal’s behalf as the principal would judge best. This approach stresses the deeply normative character of corrigibility, while remaining sufficiently concrete so as to be specifiable formally. In this article, I lay out the central problem of corrigibility, elucidate the issues with existing approaches, and clarify the conceptual ingredients of my new framework. I then present an initial formalism , proving theorem-level guarantees about agents pursuing the goal in three increasingly realistic formal settings. Finally, I address some limitations of the picture as presented and outline further research directions that this work points toward. From normative learning to corrigibility The complete normative learning problem Suppose you are designing a powerful AI and you need to choose which goals the AI should pursue, at whatever level of specification you can provide. Doing this well demands answers to a number of normative problems: what constitutes a right decision, what factors should be considered in the process of valuing the world, how the AI ought to act, etc. In some sense the ideal AI directive would be to figure out and then pursue the Good, a universal-best-interests type of goal that can only be acquired through normative learning . The challenge of describing such a learner is one formulation of what I'd call the central problem of outer alignment : what would be the overall best goal for an AI to pursue? The complete version of this problem is very difficult, and it runs up against our own deepest questions about human ethics, values, and interests. Discussing this problem formally is especially difficult: the rich truth of human normativity seems to resist systematic formalization at the level of individual recommendations for action. [1] A formalism requires an operationalization, a way to concretely specify the concept of right action at least to some degree. For any hope at concreteness, we need a clearer formulation of the overall goal. A first attempt might be something like "the promotion of overall human flourishing", centering a thick normative concept about humanity that must be defined further. In trying to pin down the meaning of human flourishing, or any other thick human concept we want to use for the goal, the most important ingredient in the AI's consideration should naturally be the interests, feelings, and inner lives of human beings. But we should be careful not to crudely use human opinion as a proxy for human best interests. Humanity cannot always accurately understand its own full best interests, and humans who cannot speak for themselves must still have their interests included in the goal. The complete normative goal cannot be constructed by treating existing human feedback as the sole source of truth. This issue is a central limitation of modern Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback, which takes static human approval or disapproval as constitutive of correct evaluation for any question without a verifiable answer. For example, a judicial AI built to decide legal cases should not exhibit any form of the hungry judge effect , where leniency depends on mealtimes. An RLHF judge will pick up on all the patterns of human imperfection, whereas an ideal AI would be one that can transcend human limitations, without discarding the fundamentally human essence of the legal system. An ideal normative AI is one fully immersed in our existing normative practices of judgment, able to deeply understand the relevant human concepts and use its intelligence to extend them to novel cases. For the complete normative learning problem, a better formulation of the target would therefore involve some idealized version of the judgment of humanity. [2] This is also already how we, as humans, reason about our own overall best interests. For example, consider a smoker whose nicotine dependence makes him crave cigarettes. At a base level, he has an interest in smoking now to avoid some physical discomfort and obtain some relief. But it's clear that the health costs he incurs as a consequence give a good reason to say that smoking is in fact not in his overall interest, assuming he values his own life and health. Neither of these reasons is dispositive; in a single case it might be that he has a reason to smoke because this particular cigarette is necessary to get him through the day or because he is old with a short remaining lifespan regardless, but he might also have a reason not to smoke because he publicly swore off cigarettes once and for all. Understanding whether it's truly better to smoke or not requires aggregating and squaring all the smoker's countervailing normative interests bearing on the subject. Any conception of value based on something like preference satisfaction involves a similar question: how should we reconcile the smoker's preference to smoke with his preference to not be dependent on nicotine anymore, along with all his other relevant preferences? A serious account of "best interests" requires this sort of reflective idealization through an accounting of reasons. Three kinds of uncertainty The moral notion of human best interests can be consequentialized , i.e., conceived of as a betterness ordering on worlds. If that ordering is total, transitive and suitably continuous, it can be represented by a utility function that takes in all the information about a world and its history as input so that a world is better exactly when the function's output is greater. We can then think of an AI as a bounded reasoner, evaluating normative questions by estimating the outputs of this function for the possible consequences of its actions. A bounded normative learner faces three kinds of uncertainty in performing this estimation: logical uncertainty about the logical consequences of existing beliefs and the results of computations, empirical uncertainty about which world it finds itself in, normative uncertainty , about which worlds are actually better than which. These correspond to the three sources of feedback the reasoner encounters: deductions of theorems in logic and mathematics, observations of the world, and human judgments about normative matters. title: A Simpler and Better Debate Protocol for Scalable Oversight
raw_summary: Linkpost to arXiv: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02557 Summary: One promising approach to scalable oversight is AI debate , which seeks to leverage a debate between two powerful AIs to break complex questions down into simpler claims that can be easily judged directly. Theoretical work on debate aims to design protocols (i.e., rules of the debate game) that provide rigorous guarantees on correctness, and the current best protocol works for all problems that have sufficiently stable decompositions into subproblems. We design a new protocol, FBS Debate, for this same class of problems that improves on the prior work: correctness holds in a worst-case rather than an average-case sense, and for a stronger equilibrium concept. We also prove that no protocol for this class of problems can outperform FBS Debate while treating human judgment as a black box. Introduction As the tasks performed by AI systems grow in complexity, it becomes increasingly difficult to provide reliable verifiable rewards that capture all relevant aspects of the task. These difficulties lead to the problem of scalable oversight : the design of training protocols that leverage the power of rapidly improving AI systems in order to augment human abilities to provide accurate training supervision to these same systems. One of the primary approaches to scalable oversight is AI debate , where two powerful AI systems argue about the correctness of an AI output, and a human judges the outcome. A debate protocol is a set of rules for how the two AIs interact and how the judge scores the interaction. The idea is that having an adversarial debater point out flaws can allow the judge to better recognize the flaws. The rules of the interaction in such protocols usually specify that the debaters must break the problem down into simpler subproblems and recursively argue about their correctness, until the original problem has been broken down to a level that is simple enough for a human to judge directly. The goal is to design these rules so that the optimal strategy leads to the judge correctly deciding the solution to the original problem (which by itself was too complex to judge). We can then use debate during RL training, in order to provide a strong supervision signal for superhuman AIs. However, debate faces a major obstacle known as the obfuscated arguments problem , where one debater can efficiently produce a dishonest argument which cannot be efficiently refuted by their opponent. One way around obfuscated arguments, already suggested in the post that introduced the problem , is to keep rejecting every false claim while only requiring the protocol to accept true claims that have a robust argument. Prover-estimator debate takes this route: it avoids obfuscated arguments for problems that admit sufficiently stable decompositions, but provides average-case guarantees that hold for a weaker equilibrium concept than previously studied. In the same theoretical model, our paper achieves stronger guarantees with a much simpler protocol, FBS Debate , which is therefore more practical to run. Furthermore, we show that FBS Debate is optimal on every individual question: unless further assumptions are made about human judgments, no other protocol can find a flawed sub-claim asymptotically more efficiently. The FBS Debate Protocol TL;DR: FBS Debate is simple to describe. The first debater, Alice, decomposes the original claim into sub-claims. The second debater, Bob, then has two choices: either (1) demonstrate that Alice’s decomposition is too sensitive to small errors in the sub-claims, or (2) choose a sub-claim on which to continue the debate recursively. As a motivating example, consider an autonomous AI agent, Alice, tasked with completing a research project in the quantitative social sciences, and another AI, Bob, who attempts to find flaws. To check a claim in her paper, we ask Alice to decompose it into sub-claims, which we can think of as pieces of supporting evidence. For example, the claim might be that a certain statistical modeling assumption is justified, and we would believe it if 50 out of 99 correct, published papers in the literature supported it. Each sub-claim then says: this particular paper is correct and supports the original claim. Now consider two things Alice might claim: Suppose Alice claims that of the papers support the claim. The key insight is that Bob need not check every paper. He can just sample one at random from the that Alice says support the claim. If Alice is lying, then at least of the sub-claims must also be lies, so Bob has a chance of catching her. Checking just a few papers is enough for Bob to be confident of catching a lie. On the other hand, suppose Alice claims that exactly 50 out of 99 papers support the claim. Now Bob has to check every one of the 50 papers, since a single incorrect paper would flip the majority vote. The key to FBS Debate is that Bob is allowed to show that Alice has made an unreasonably sensitive claim of this form, in which case Alice loses the debate. Indeed, one should be very suspicious of any argument that is highly sensitive to changes in individual pieces of evidence, yet relies on fuzzy human judgments at each step. The majority-vote example, assuming Alice is lying. The notion of fractional block sensitivity (FBS) generalizes the intuition above about majority vote to any way Alice might combine her sub-claims. If the fractional block sensitivity of Alice’s decomposition is low, Bob can efficiently select a sub-claim that has a non-trivial chance of being incorrect. The debate then recurses on the sub-claim Bob samples, until a human judge directly evaluates the final selected sub-claim. To avoid losing immediately, Alice must keep the fractional block sensitivity of every decomposition low. So if Bob samples this way at every level, each run of the debate has a non-trivial chance of catching a lying Alice. Building on this, Bob can amplify his chance of catching Alice through repetition. Since we assume the debaters themselves know the answers to these final, human-judgeable claims, Bob can simply run many debate rollouts on his own, and if he finds one in which Alice made an incorrect human-judgeable claim, he reveals that claim to the judge, so the judge only needs to evaluate a single claim. With enough rollouts, he catches a lying Alice with high probability. Viewed from the lens of practical AI debate, this represents a trade-off between allowing highly sensitive arguments and the inference-time computation required to verify them. FBS Debate. Top: one round at level . Bottom: the recursion for levels. See the paper for a detailed explanation. Honesty is the best policy In FBS Debate, honest play is the best strategy for each debater, no matter what the other does: if the original claim is correct, an honest Alice always wins, and if it is incorrect, an honest Bob wins with overwhelming probability. By contrast, prover-estimator debate only guarantees that for any dishonest strategy Alice picks, Bob has some winning strategy, which can depend on Alice’s strategy in complicated ways. This is a much weaker condition, and in practice training toward the equilibrium of FBS Debate is much more stable and tractable. Furthermore, FBS Debate applies on a worst-case basis: prover-estimator debate only works on average over a distribution of questions, while FBS Debate guarantees that on each individual question, honesty is the best policy. Optimality We show that, on each individual question, no protocol that treats human judgment as a black box can find a flawed sub-claim asymptotically more efficiently than FBS Debate.
