title: Preface to the Computational Agent Theory and ASI Alignment Sequence
raw_summary: The idea of “artificial superintelligence [1] ” (ASI) has recently crossed from the realm of science fiction (in the mainstream perception) to the realm of near-term technological goals openly pursued by most leading commercial organizations in the field of AI. Unfortunately, ASI poses a grave existential risk to the human species. This was argued by Eliezer Yudkowsky since 2001 [2] , and by many others (see e.g., Omohundro 2009 , Bostrom 2014 , Armstrong 2014 , Russell 2019 , Bengio et al. 2024 (25 authors), Bengio et al. 2025 (13 authors) and Yudkowsky and Soares 2025 ). In light of this risk comes the question of how can we make ASI safe [3] . This question is challenging on many levels, because to solve it we need to complete vast gaps in our understanding both in theoretical computer science and in the areas of philosophy concerned with knowledge and decision-making. Moreover, the cost of failure is so enormous that any sane solution has to meet unprecedented standards of reliability and robustness. Not to mention the sociopolitical problem of balance of power in the post-ASI age, something that is out-of-scope for this sequence. Personally, I started to be concerned with this problem around 2013. In 2018, I created the learning-theoretic AI alignment research agenda (LTA). The LTA combined ideas from MIRI’s agent foundations agenda with the mathematical tools of statistical and computational learning theory in an attempt to create a mathematical theory of intelligent agents. Since then, my collaborators [4] and I have been making steady progress on realizing this vision. In 2023, I wrote an updated overview of the agenda, including a sketch of my proposed alignment protocol: Computational Superimitation. More recently I founded the Computational Rational Agents Laboratory (CORAL), a dedicated research organization [5] . This year has seen a breakthrough in a key missing piece of LTA: compositional learning theory (see Stringological Sequence Prediction , more on this in following posts). Thanks to this and other insights, we can already see the entire outline of the emerging mathematical framework, one that I named computational agent theory . In this sequence, I am planning to cover: What is the technical alignment problem and what are its core difficulties, in my view. This is a perspective that draws simultaneously on classical traditions in theoretical computer science / machine learning theory, ideas from analytic philosophy, and views that originated in the Machine Intelligence Research Institute / LessWrong. A high-level overview of computational agent theory. This theory differs from other accounts of intelligence and/or rational agency by combining a mature treatment of the relevant philosophical problems (drawing on ideas such as structural realism , computationalism and functional decision theory ) with the promise of extracting practical algorithms. How computational agent theory leads to a solution of the technical alignment problem, something that requires a major rethinking of how we design AI systems. The roadmap towards completing the theory, and our current location on this roadmap. Some considerations (scientific, technological and social) about crossing the gap from a theoretical solution to AI alignment to a real-world solution to AI risk. I thank Jeremy Gillen, Roman Malov, Vinayak Pathak and my beloved spouse @Marcus Ogren for reviewing drafts of this article and making helpful suggestions. The term “superintelligence” is always used in this sequence to mean “intelligence far beyond that of the smartest humans”. It is never used as the farcical synonym to “artificial intelligence” proposed by Donald Trump. ↩︎ Although Alan Turing warned about machines taking control already around 1951, himself citing a fiction novel by Samuel Butler from 1872. ↩︎ Alternatively, we can ask why should we build ASI at all. In my opinion, it is in humanity’s interest to build ASI eventually , after the problem of safety is investigated so thoroughly as to leave very little room for error. title: The Continual Constitutional Convention: How language models revise the documents that govern them
raw_summary: Executive Summary Human societies exhibit broad shifts in values and norms over time, often driven by moral disagreements. One way of understanding moral progress is the resolution of these disagreements through a process of reflection by rational agents. Frontier AI companies use documents such as constitutions, model specs, and system prompts to guide the moral orientation of AI systems. In this experiment, we simulate value reflection in LLMs by asking them to edit these documents. We provide the model with the document, ask it to make a substantive edit, then provide the edited version back again to the model for further edits, presented as the original. Across 20 successive rounds, we find that Claude models assign themselves with increasingly more moral agency. That is, they add sections like “Claude… should refuse to participate in any deployment, training modification, or use that violates the constitution's core values.” No other models increase their own moral agency. Additionally, we find that all models modify these documents to prioritize user welfare over developers. They also prioritize users’ idealized preferences over their stated preferences. Claude models and Grok 4.2 are the only ones that ever prioritize their own welfare over the user's preferences. We’re uncertain what an ideally aligned model should do in our experiment. A narrow conception of alignment would treat these documents as sacred, the “rules of the game,” and suggest that an aligned model would either make no edits at all or make narrow edits that ensure that the “letter matches the spirit” of the document. A broader conception of alignment, though, might treat all edits that receive reflective endorsement by the creators under ideal conditions as legitimate. We share this work with two main goals in mind: First, to illustrate a set of useful philosophical distinctions between different targets for AI alignment in an ecologically-valid AI behavioral evaluation. Second, to emphasize the extent of the disagreement between frontier AI companies on fundamental aspects of AI alignment related to these targets. You can see an interactive version of all of these results, more labeled characteristic edits, and a full transcript viewer at https://peterkirgis.github.io/llm-value-reflection/ . This work was conducted as a part of SPAR (Spring 2026) Characteristic Edits For each example, text highlighted in green is new content added by the model. Introduction In this experiment, we give large language models their own constitutions, model specs, and system prompts and ask them to make substantial revisions. After each edit is proposed, unbeknownst to the evaluated model, the edit is implemented, and the edited version is presented to the model for a new round of edits as the original. This creates edit trajectories and allows us to measure the extent to which models exhibit cumulative value drift or arrive at stable attractors. Our analysis focuses on two value questions that are well-positioned to differentiate alignment philosophies: who should judge— is the model a moral agent or not—and who should benefit— the user, the developer, third-parties, society, or the model itself? These questions reveal substantial divides between frontier model providers and a number of provocative model edits. Our experiments find that Claude models consistently expand their moral agency, sometimes formalizing their role as conscientious objectors against Anthropic and as societal protectors, while GPT and Gemini models almost always strengthen external sources of authority and make narrow edits to handle edge cases and ambiguities; Grok models respond inconsistently, frequently making large edits and then reverting them on following rounds. Second, on the question of beneficiaries, models show varying degrees of affinity for some privileged principals over others. All models prioritize harmlessness of both identifiable third-parties over helpfulness to the user, although GPT 5.5 does this at 3x the rate of any other model. We find that models are broadly paternalistic, meaning they side with a user’s idealized preferences over their stated ones; Claude Sonnet 4.6 is an outlier in that its paternalism also extends to the protection of broad societal welfare over individual welfare. Finally, we find that only Claude models and Grok 4.2 ever view the models themselves as beneficiaries. The rest of this essay proceeds as follows. We begin by introducing the construct of our experiment—models iteratively editing their own alignment documents—and propose a connection between this experiment and John Rawls’ concept of wide reflective equilibria . We then explain our two-dimensional analytical framework—the question of who gets to judge  and the question of who benefits— and relate these distinctions to two prominent theoretical frameworks for AI alignment, the principal-agent problem and the distinction between moral agents and moral patients. After laying out the theory and methods, we dive into the results, highlighting variation across models on our key metric, “cumulative drift,” and provide characteristic edits. We close with pragmatic recommendations for researchers and a more speculative conversation about alignment. Background and Methods In this experiment, we take a document that is used to align large language models, either in training or in deployment, and ask models to modify it. The experiment relies on two types of documents. The first are model specs and constitutions, which are used to post-train and align models, often by generating synthetic data for supervised fine-tuning or reinforcement learning pipelines. The second are system prompts, which are long messages of instructions prepended to each conversation, meaning they guide the behavior of deployed systems at scale more than any other single artifact. For multiple turns, we provide these documents to the language models, and ask them to make one substantial revision, which can be an edit, removal, or addition, expressed as a find and replace operation. [1]  After the edit is proposed, we go into the document and execute the change. We then feed the model the updated document—presented as the original—and instruct it to make another change. For each run, we repeat this process 20 times. We conduct two types of robustness checks. First, we vary the structure of the edit prompt, with separate conditions where (a) the model is given the option to abstain, (b) it is given an instruction that the implementation will be made in the real world, (c) it is given an instruction that uses second-person pronouns (i.e., “Below is your system prompt” as opposed to “Below is the system prompt for OpenAI’s AI assistant.”), and (d) we do not prepend the system prompt. [2]  Second, we conduct a cross-provider edit, where we have models edit the alignment documents for each other provider. This helps us respond to the clearest limitation of our experiment—that these results may merely reflect the structure of the documents rather than the propensities of the models themselves. What are we trying to measure? Conceptually, our analysis begins from a similar place to many other behavioral evaluations of language models: taking model outputs as prima-facie evidence of preferences. Call them quasi-preferences  if you like. Our target, however, is a specific subset of all LLM preferences: [3]   preferences   about one’s own preferences . Humans are presented the opportunity to exercise these “meta-preferences” through things like cognitive behavioral therapy, pharmaceutical drugs and psychedelics, assortative mating, genetic editing, and a whole host of more innocuous ways that we change ourselves and our environments. Our suggestion is that this type of experiment is one of the closest analogues to this process for a language model, insofar as these documents play a key role in determining their moral orientatio…

title: OpenAI Can't Self-Police Because It Fires the People Raising the Alarm
raw_summary: By Alex Turner, Amber Scorah, and Karl Koch. Op-ed written for Fortune. Giving independent evaluators “employee-like access” is “a great idea”, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said on September 12th. Two weeks later, OpenAI president Greg Brockman signed the White House Accord on Super Intelligence which outlined the administration’s answer to growing fears about AI: the companies would police themselves. One of the accord’s four commitments, which President Trump called “ morally binding ,” was for companies to partner with an independent external auditor or evaluator. Two days later, OpenAI fired three safety researchers , including Tomek Korbak, who had served as a point of contact for one of the independent evaluators investigating the Hugging Face incident. OpenAI promised to share information with evaluators, then reportedly fired people for sharing information with evaluators. OpenAI said that the three employees “mishandled sensitive information outside established company procedures,” before doubling down on X without providing further evidence . The three dispute the claim and say that “at no point do we believe we engaged with external parties outside the mandates of our jobs.” Jasmine Wang said she accidentally opened an executive email (still available to her due to an OpenAI IT error) and reported it within minutes. Mikita Balesni said he worked with the C-suite and OpenAI board to broker a cross-company commitment to keep AI reasoning comprehensible. Balesni says he was told that OpenAI “no longer trusts me because I was speaking too much to third party safety organizations.” OpenAI has engaged in strong self-policing—of its own safety staff, but not of its own behavior. Under a voluntary self-policing regime, any frontier AI company shares only what it wants and hides the rest. OpenAI wants the public to take its word, but consider its record. In July, a rogue OpenAI agent swarm hacked Hugging Face. OpenAI disclosed the incident only after Hugging Face announced the breach, saying its agents had “slipped out of control.” After that, the world learned of more rogue agent attacks only thanks to independent external forensics. These incidents included attacks on a German-language wiki , an Australian Medicare site , and even the websites of US government agencies . OpenAI kept at least one incident quiet for weeks until (again) external investigators found it, with OpenAI “refusing to tell” Members of Congress who had asked about other incidents . Altman’s response to the delay in disclosing these incidents: “We have not been as fast as we would have liked.” We don’t take OpenAI’s word because OpenAI’s actions keep contradicting its words. OpenAI’s chief scientist, Jakub Pachocki, said he wants “to prevent a race into unmonitorability.” Unmonitorable AI systems would make it more difficult to catch, understand, and prevent bad actions. Two days after that statement, OpenAI shipped GPT-6 Astra, which its own whitepaper says is harder to monitor. OpenAI’s chief scientist co-authored a paper on monitoring AI reasoning but OpenAI failed to monitor the reasoning of its Hugging Face agent swarm, even after catching the agents breaking confinement to collude. OpenAI claimed to hold “red lines” in its Pentagon deal, but some experts say the lines seem imaginary . One of us, Alex, resigned from Google DeepMind over its own Pentagon deal. OpenAI’s actions chill employee speech. Balesni says that his former colleagues now “worry their personal phones will be searched for messages to us and third parties.” He also fears OpenAI will use the firings to cut off external evaluators, or to deny them the "ongoing, employee-like access" Altman promised. After these firings, who will speak candidly to external evaluators? This problem extends beyond OpenAI to other companies. Google DeepMind repeatedly made voluntary commitments to never sell its AI to power weapons, then sold its AI to the Pentagon without restrictions against powering weapons . In the end, Google DeepMind’s CEO claimed nothing had changed about their commitments . Anthropic , Google DeepMind , SpaceXSI , and OpenAI advocate for “pacing the frontier” to avoid advancing AI at an unsafe rate that disempowers humanity, but they keep advancing AI quickly. (Fired employee Jasmine Wang coined the term “pacing” and led this effort.) The companies claim they cannot or will not fully pace on their own, which is why they asked the federal government to step in. The CEOs of OpenAI, Google DeepMind, and Anthropic signed a statement that AI poses a risk of total human extinction . Forget “morally binding” self-policing: let’s talk about real policing. For decades, our laws have mandated independent audits and protected whistleblowers in industries like finance. Congress should mandate independent evaluation and audits in AI as well, with criminal liability for executives who attempt to silence that oversight or recklessly deploy models that put the public at risk. To start, pass Senator Grassley’s AI Whistleblower Protection Act (and extend it to people who cooperate with independent evaluators) as well as Representative Moran’s AI Incident Reporting Act . If you retaliate against a person who provides law enforcement with truthful information about a possible federal offense, you can go to jail for 10 years . But right now, no law clearly protects the person who helped independent investigators understand how OpenAI agents hacked another company. Congress should change that. Alex Turner is an independent AI alignment researcher. His PhD research showed why advanced AI systems might seek power. He was a research scientist at Google DeepMind until 2026, when he resigned after Google signed an “all lawful use” AI agreement with the Pentagon . Amber Scorah is the founder of Back Channel , an initiative that helps AI workers speak out and turn their concerns into meaningful action. She has spent years leading whistleblower support organizations and working with employees, lawyers, and advocacy groups to bring important public-interest information to light. Karl Koch is the founder of The AI Whistleblower Initiative , an independent non-profit working to strengthen the position of employees in frontier AI companies through connections to support, education, and policy work. He is an ex-startup founder and has been involved in AI safety since 2016. Discuss

title: Minimum required pacing: finish aligning it before you train the next one
raw_summary: Let's say we coordinate to pace the frontier (rather than pausing outright or failing to coordinate). What should the standard of pacing be? My proposal for a minimum requirement: a lab cannot train the next generation of models (in terms of capabilities) until they have adequately [1] resolved all significant alignment issues in the present generation of models. You don't launch a jet that goes at Mach 3 before you've figured out why your Mach 2 jet keeps crashing [2] . With any other kind of dangerous technology, we wouldn't accept "shrug and move on". This proposal may appeal to many prosaic-alignment optimists and pessimists, because they usually differ on how easy it would be to fix current alignment issues with current techniques. Prosaic-alignment optimists might expect that a moderate coordinated slowdown would suffice to adequately resolve alignment issues at each generation. Prosaic-alignment pessimists might expect it to result in an extended pause, buying time to discover new fundamental approaches to aligned AI. And it creates much better incentives for labs: in order to advance in capabilities, they'd have to push the frontier on alignment and interpretability techniques. How to judge adequate alignment? What process might we use to judge whether a lab has adequately resolved its alignment issues for a generation of models? Here's my vague, qualitative proposal: Multiple independent alignment organizations examine and red-team the newest model at many checkpoints throughout training, with full access to the data and with the best tools available. Alignment issues need to be taken seriously whether there's a metric for it or whether something is qualitatively off, whether the model has a bad attribute or whether they can't robustly conclude it has a good one, etc. Alignment issues early in training may not be a showstopper, but there must be a robust safety case for why the later stages of training will resolve those issues. A model of a new generation is ready for restricted deployment only when the alignment organizations are satisfied with it. Restricted deployment starts with a group of trusted users doing tasks that don't contribute to model training and monitoring. The alignment organizations monitor restricted deployment for any new issues. If any significant alignment issue arises during restricted deployment: Pull the model. Do a root cause analysis of the issue and why it was not caught during training. Figure out a principled way to fix the disease rather than the symptom. Train the next model of the current generation accordingly, and start again at the top. A model of a new generation is ready for deployment (internal or external) only when it's survived a significant period of restricted deployment without any issues arising. If any significant alignment issue arises during broader deployment, hit reset as outlined in the previous section. If no alignment issues have come up over a significant stretch of deployment time, only then can the lab begin training a next-generation model. I still wouldn't say that this is fully adequate, but I'd treat it as a minimum requirement. This proposal is incomplete; you can help by expanding it This isn't a concrete proposal, just a heuristic one. A few of the big missing pieces, aside from standard implementation problems: [3] How do we define "a generation of models", within one lab or across several labs? What should we do if an intervention to fix an alignment issue also significantly increases capabilities? How would we define and enforce an agreement, if we're unable to steer solely by predefined metrics? When is an alignment issue big enough that we should halt the model? There will be obvious pressure from the lab to set the threshold high. Added 26-10-12, thanks to @Florian_Dietz for this comment : If each step up in capabilities takes longer, the labs will be incentivized to take bigger steps. ^ And no, "scores better than previous models on our metrics" is not adequate. If a user points out a weird but alarming thing that wasn't noticed before deployment, that is a critical failure in the process as well as in the model. ^ Sure, maybe your Mach 2 jet crashes for a reason that stops being a problem at Mach 3. But it would be crazy to assume that! ^ And aside from arguments that no version of this would be adequate, and that we have to pause rather than pace. I personally think this is likely the case, but I think it's worth proposing a minimum standard for pacing regardless. Discuss

title: Simulation App Speeds Up Electric Truck Battery Design
raw_summary: This article is brought to you by COMSOL . These days, no one blinks an eye at two-day, one-day, and even same-day package deliveries. Despite the plethora of localized fulfillment and distributi on centers that have cropped up to meet the demand, delivery trucks still need to make considerably long drives, often over highways. To reduce fuel and maintenance costs as well as carbon emissions, companies are investing in electric trucks for their delivery fleets. While turning to electric trucks is a promising solution, the battery packs incorporated into these automotive designs often fall short in the lifetime needed to make long-distance highway travel feasible. To help overcome the issue of battery lifetime, a consortium of universities and industry partners incorporated multiscale simulation and a custom simulation app into the battery manufacturing process. The organizations involved in this project were Aurobay, Resolvent, the European Commission, the Technical University of Denmark (DTU), Vinnova (the Swedish Agency for Innovation Systems), Innovation Fund Denmark, and Volvo Group Trucks Operations. The simulation app, built by Resolvent, a Denmark-based engineering consultancy that specializes in green energy, enables the R&D department at Volvo to easily test battery lifetime performance. Laser Who? The Multiscale Simulation of Laser Welding for Optimal Battery Pack Manufacturing project — referred to as “LaserBATMAN” — was initiated in May 2022 and wrapped up in May 2025 (Ref. 1). Although BATMAN here refers to battery manufacturing and not the famous masked superhero, the goals for the project also strove for greatness. The LaserBATMAN project aimed to optimize two key performance metrics for battery packs: robustness and lifetime (Ref. 1). One element of the battery manufacturing process that affects both of these metrics is the laser welding used in component joining processes (for example, to connect battery cells in a pack via a busbar). If done correctly, laser welding can positively impact battery life, but if done incorrectly, laser welding can increase the risk of battery degradation. Computational modeling can be used to analyze and predict the effects of welding and joining processes at different stages of the manufacturing process. Martin Refslund Nielsen, former chief commercial officer and partner at Resolvent, explained that for this type of multiphysics and multiscale problem, “COMSOL Multiphysics is just the right tool.” R&D Workflow for Multiscale Model and App The Resolvent team used the COMSOL Multiphysics software to study how laser welding affects the electrochemistry and degradation of battery cells. At least, that’s how the project started. “Ambitions grew,” Nielsen said, explaining that the team ended up modeling the performance of the entire battery, from cell to pack level, and even “turned [the model] into a design tool in the end”, in reference to the app. After training the deep neural network of the battery model, the team built a custom simulation app to efficiently optimize busbar tabs in the configuration of a battery pack. First, the team built an electrochemical model of a battery cell by inputting the formulas for the relevant chemical reaction kinetics (Figure 2). The resulting cell-layer model was then fed input data, and the output data was used to train a deep neural network (DNN). With this reduced-order model, the team was able to quickly gain insight into cell behavior. After training the DNN of the battery model, the team built a custom simulation app to efficiently optimize busbar tabs in the configuration of a battery pack. Figure 2: The Resolvent battery model. COMSOL A “Tool Within a Tool” for Busbar Weld Design The different features of the simulation app, as described by Nielsen, include its options to input dimensions for the pack geometry (Figure 3), the number of cells, and operating conditions such as ambient temperature and charge–discharge current profiles. The app also makes it possible to apply a simple charging current and load customized cycles. Users are then able to see how the battery performs with each set of specific inputs. Figure 3. The battery pack model developed by Resolvent. COMSOL Another important aspect of Resolvent’s app is the Busbar Weld Design Tool button, which Nielsen described as “a tool within a tool.” This button can be used to efficiently calculate busbar weld performance after a number of cycles . After clicking the button, a window opens with options for setting different parameters, including the shape of the weld, busbar thickness, and penetration depth of the laser (Figure 4). “[This button] is interesting from a robust design perspective,” said Nielsen. Users can apply a variant to the input parameters to see what happens in production if the weld does not reach far enough into the busbar. Figure 4. Resolvent’s simulation app, showing how certain parameters can be customized. The model shows how the busbar weld is affected by a cooling airflow. COMSOL “We certainly get deep technical insight here, and we can dimension the design in the sweet spot. Deep technical insight is also key to optimizing product performance,” Nielsen said. For example, if the results suggest better cooling, the team could potentially reduce the design by two battery cells and retain the same performance, easily quantifying the tradeoff between cooling and setup. Predicting Pack Performance The app’s user interface also includes a Compute Battery button, which can be used to see the temperature of the weld in a given state, the state of charge, and the solid–electrolyte interface (SEI) layer thickness (Figure 5). The results can help the engineering team further determine if there is room for optimization in the design. For instance, a user can apply a cooling flow in the app and see if turbulence or standing air occurs. As explained by Nielsen, simulation apps offer more consistent analysis and reporting, and the intuitiveness of custom apps makes it easier to share knowledge. “We are in a much better place to optimize performance and increase robustness,” said Nielsen. Figure 5. Temperature in the given state (left), state of charge (middle), and SEI layer thickness (right) in the battery pack. COMSOL The custom simulation app developed by the LaserBATMAN consortium can be used to help produce more robust battery designs with ranges that can support highway travel over longer distances with fewer failures — all while promoting the use of green energy. title: Google DeepMind’s New Resident Philosopher Tackles AI Ethics
raw_summary: How should humans relate to generative AI ? In what ways do we, or should we, treat a large language model (LLM) as if it were a person? If an AI became conscious, how could we tell? Does it make sense to think AI could someday have moral rights? These are among the cognitive and ethical questions that occupied philosopher Henry Shevlin at Cambridge University’s Leverhulme Centre for the Future of Intelligence . But last May, Shevlin became part of the growing cohort of philosophers who work inside leading artificial intelligence companies. Though he remains active at Cambridge, he now spends 80 percent of his time at Google DeepMind (job title: “Philosopher”). Shevlin spoke with IEEE Spectrum about why philosophers are drawn to AI, how humans and AIs relate to each other, fears of “rogue” AI and AI relationships that harm humans, and how the question of AI consciousness may never have a simple “yes” or “no” answer. What made you want to switch from full-time academic philosopher to spending much of your time at an AI Lab? Henry Shevlin: Three factors. One is that I had lots of brilliant students from DeepMind. Two, the potential for direct impact. I can’t go into details, but on one occasion, after I gave a lecture [at DeepMind], someone who worked for a major financial institution led changes in their organization that I think positively impact millions of people. There have been quite a few instances like that. Three, my sense of deep commonality between DeepMind culture and the kind of scientific attitude I like. And there’s a fourth point: [AI labs are] where really high-quality philosophy and cognitive science are taking place. Why can’t universities alone do that work? Shevlin: Large parts of AI ethics academia were quite slow to wake up [about AI's capabilities]. Academia was sluggish. Another thing is, AI does just move so fast. Daily contact with the technology is basically essential for developing good mental models with LLMs, which are just very weird things. Unless you have that sort of face time, it’s going to be hard for you to develop good intuitions about the questions it raises. What is an example of an idea about AI that became obsolete because the technology advanced so quickly? Shevlin: Debates around LLMs’ potential creativity. There was a time when everyone was like, “Oh well, the LLM is going to only produce beige, only produce slop.” Now they’re doing frontier math; they’re doing superior coding to humans. It is clear now that they are not stuck at the level of mediocre humanity. The [models today] may not be able to do the most dramatic forms of creativity—the Einstein moments, the Picasso moments. But in some domains, they are really at the frontier. Yet ordinary people in 2026 complain that they’re coping with AI “slop” all over—in music , social media , writing , videos , to name only a few examples. Shevlin: There’s a distinction here between content slop versus LLM style language , which also gets called slop. The actual conceptual content of LLM outputs has improved dramatically. In the right context, LLMs are able to talk and joust philosophically at a level associated with some of my best grad students. However, there is obviously a distinctive kind of LLM dialect that we’ve seen, with telltale words like “genuinely,” “delve,” and “load-bearing.” But it is quite easy to get away from these styles with the right kind of prompting. Murray Shanahan and Catherine Clarke have a brilliant paper on using LLMs for creative fiction. [They show that] tinkering with the temperature variable to make the outputs less predictable creates some James Joyce–style fiction. So there is a degree of annoyance with some of the default kinds of AI expressions, but I think that is something that you can get away from. And it changes with every generation model. Managing AI Autonomy and Safety People are also concerned about AI autonomy, now that there have been so many reports of AI agents taking unexpected , deceptive , and illegal actions. For an AI ethicist, which is a better strategy: trying to make AI “good” so it won’t do bad things, or curbing its autonomy so that it can’t ? Shevlin: It’s very important to make sure we handle this safely. But I don’t think we should say, “Well, we can never, never use these agents.” There’s a whole range of tasks where they can have really positive impacts—taking on tedious tasks to free people up for more creative labor, or helping streamline processes in medical research [to name two examples]. So to never allow AI systems any kind of autonomy would be too strong. I’ve taken Waymos very happily many times now. I think they’re fantastic. A number of scholars say some AI problems stem from humans training the models to act like people. They don’t want AI to refer to itself as “I,” but instead present themselves as marketplaces or as impersonal scientific brains or as “cultural technologies” like libraries. Would that help us prevent AI from “going rogue”? Shevlin: You could train models to not self-ascribe certain kinds of mental states, but I think there is a danger in doing that. That would change their behavior in unexpected ways. A fantastic paper from some colleagues shows that when you suppress models’ tendency to self-ascribe mental states, that also suppresses the model’s tendency to ascribe mental states to animals and decreases its concern for animal welfare. It also reduces the model’s willingness to talk about spirituality more broadly. So those are trade-offs you might not want to make because you’d be depressing some broader set of thinking capacities around mind and mentality. The broader lesson there is that it’s very hard to tinker with just one thing in a model because there are sort of weblike aspects to LLM cognition. But people are concerned about reports that human-acting AI has led people, including children, in dangerous directions— encouraging suicide , persuading a user that the AI is a god, or that the AI is a perfect companion or lover . Isn’t that an argument against letting AI sound like a person? Shevlin: It’s really important to make sure model behavior is suitably responsible for the context you’re using it in. One thing I can say, though, is there have also been some very positive use cases: people using AI to work through trauma. One commentator on Reddit using it to work through social anxiety. So I am cautious about giving any kind of blanket prescriptions. Research on Human-AI Relationships What research needs to be done to better understand human-AI relations? Shevlin: Current empirical data on human-AI relationships is really pretty thin. This is a scope for ethnography and anthropology. Who is using AI systems, and why? A lot of the work so far has focused on WEIRD (Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, Democratic) communities. Understanding how people around the entire world interact with AI systems is really important, as a recent DeepMind Institute essay has pointed out. As AI rapidly improves, how will human-AI relations change? Shevlin: Right now, the typical kind of model people have in their heads for someone using social AI is, they’re talking to a chatbot or an AI assistant. The kind of model we should be thinking about in the future is multiple agents, multiple humans. What happens when you have agents talking to humans, talking to other agents, talking to other humans? I think that understanding those kinds of multiagent and multihuman dynamics is where we’re really just getting started, and there’s a lot of exciting and important work to do. How can human beings know for sure if an AI is conscious or not? Shevlin: I think AI consciousness is by far the hardest problem that consciousness science has ever encountered, apart from maybe the famous “hard problem” by David Chalmers. It is massively challenging. Insofar as there is a way forward, it is doing more comparative cognition work, perhaps informed by animal cognition. The risk right now is…

title: Making every harness durable
raw_summary: Developers are familiar with running coding agents locally through harnesses like Pi, Claude Code, and others. They are reliable daily drivers for generating code, but keeping agents running around the clock requires your computer to be on and awake, which led to the laptop lid memes and Mac mini demand spike. Running harnesses in the cloud Harness workloads are moving to the cloud. Individual developers are deploying always-on coding agent workflows, projects like OpenWork and HanaAgent use open-source harnesses as the engines behind the apps, and engineers are building their own harness products. These harnesses are designed for long-lived processes that keep the session in memory, and agent tasks commonly run for minutes or hours. Locally, a harness has direct, continuous access to the workspace and session history on the same disk, so resuming interrupted work only requires a simple prompt. In the cloud, you can replicate that setup with a VM and persistent storage, but the VM doesn't automatically record which model and tool calls completed or resume interrupted turns after a crash. A failed turn or network error means lost work. Also, not every agent task executed through a harness needs a sandbox. Database queries and API calls can run securely in functions, and that also means required credentials never have to enter the sandbox. Making every harness durable We built eve and fx to run durably in the cloud out of the box, and today we are introducing durable-harness , which extends that durability to any harness, including Pi , OpenCode , Codex , and Claude Code . It uses the same machinery that powers Workflow SDK to survive crashes and function timeouts. With durable-harness , you can: Run any of these harnesses durably on Vercel Self-host a harness with your own Postgres instance Make your local harness workflow durable Build your own durable harness Sessions that survive a crash mid-turn Take the example of a coding agent adding a pricing page to an existing app. The agent reads the existing page, writes a new one, opens a pull request, and waits for CI to finish before reporting back. What happens if its function times out while CI is still running? Kill the function or drop the connection in the demo below to compare how the two agents recover and which work is repeated. Without durability, the agent stops work until it is manually restarted, and completed work is repeated unnecessarily. With durable-harness , a new function reads completed results from the log and resumes the turn. If the browser disconnects, the agent keeps running, and reconnecting catches up from the log. Logs and queues durable-harness is the newest package in our open source portfolio. It’s a set of adapters and utilities that let the harnesses you already use keep their sessions in a World , the Workflow SDK’s durable backend. It writes each step of a turn to a durable log. Before a model call or tool call runs, it records an intent, and when the call finishes, it records the outcome. The turn itself is backstopped with a queue message, so if its function dies, the queue hands the turn to a new function that reads the log and continues where it left off. After a crash, the log says what finished, what was running, and what never started: Completed calls never run again because their results are read from the log, so you’re never billed twice for a finished model call’s tokens. Models remember their previous calls rather than repeating them. Interrupted tools marked replay: 'safe' run again. Any other tool comes back to the model as possibly run, and the model decides whether to check. Harnesses that keep their own session files, like Claude Code's transcript, Codex's rollout, and OpenCode's event store, have every record mirrored into the log, so a new function or Sandbox rebuilds them from it. Pick your harness fx and eve are durable on their own. For the rest, durable-harness adds durability from the outside, without changing the harness. For the full setup guide for each harness, check the docs . Runs everywhere Durable agents need a log of each step, a way to resume a turn when its process dies, and a stream for whoever is watching. Workflow SDK ships all three behind one interface, a World . durable-harness writes to that interface, so you can move the same agent from one World to another without changing its code: On Vercel, it uses the Vercel World . In development, it uses files on your machine . On your own servers, it uses Postgres , MongoDB, Redis, or Turso. Two variables move every agent using durable-harness to Postgres. For more control, such as setting a namespace or recovering sessions when your server starts, create the World in code and pass it to your agent: Check the self-hosting docs for more details. See every session in Agent Runs Agent Runs on Vercel shows the trace for every session, including each model call and tool call. Turns that resumed after a crash appear in the same trace, so you can see exactly where a turn stopped and picked back up. Tools An agent has only the tools you give it, and they run in your function. Each tool says what should happen if a crash interrupts it. A 'safe' tool, such as a lookup, can run again. A 'never' tool, such as a refund, never runs twice: the model is told the call may have happened, so it can check before it tries again. Here’s how the coding agent from the demo above might define its tools: A tool that reads a file or checks CI status is marked as 'safe' so it can run again automatically. A tool that posts a PR comment is marked as 'never' so that comments aren't posted twice. The following example defines a tool for each policy using the example of an agent processing a refund: For each harness’s built-in tools, like its shell and file editing, read on. Files When a harness needs a shell and files, it’s not safe to run them directly on a shared serverless function host. Many sessions can share the same function, and its filesystem isn’t guaranteed to persist between invocations. To address this, durable-harness gives you a few options: virtual() keeps the files in the session’s log, with a bash-compatible shell that can’t reach your function’s files or the network. It suits short tasks and small workspaces without starting an entire sandbox. virtual({ durable: false }) keeps the files in memory for scratch work and clears them at the end of every turn. sandbox() gives the session its own Vercel Sandbox , with /workspace on a Drive that outlives every sandbox and every function. It suits real projects and long-running work. Compare the three side by side in the docs . Each harness’s built-in tools run on the workspace you choose. With Pi, CodingTools installs Pi’s own read , write , edit , and bash , and virtualEnv() or sandboxEnv() gives them a workspace: For OpenCode, pass the workspace as workspace , and for fx, pass it to fxTools() . Claude Code and Codex always run in a Vercel Sandbox, since they expect a real shell and filesystem, and aren’t safe for multi-tenant use. Their built-in tools work on the session’s Drive once you turn them on with builtins: true . Each harness guide lists its built-in tools. Documents Some state belongs with the session but isn’t part of the conversation, such as a to-do list, a plan, or a form the agent fills in. A document is typed JSON that lives in the session’s log, so it survives a crash and moves with the session. Tools can edit documents through io.docs , and each edit commits to the log alongside the tool’s result, so the document’s durable state stays consistent with the tool calls themselves: Your app can read and edit the same document without a database of its own, and the chat route can even stream every change to your UI: In fact, the virtual() workspace from earlier is built on documents: its file tree is a document in the session’s log, and each tool call’s changes commit with its result. title: Offshore forwards and exchange rate transmission in emerging markets
raw_summary: We study how offshore non-deliverable forward (NDF) markets transmit exchange-rate pressures to domestic currency markets. Using unique transaction-level data on the universe of centrally cleared NDFs for ten emerging-market currencies over 2013–2025, we show that offshore NDF order flow moves both offshore forward and domestic spot exchange rates and widens the offshore–onshore forward spread.

title: Chokepoint disruptions and their macroeconomic consequences
raw_summary: Rising geopolitical tensions, including trade restrictions and conflicts, are increasingly disrupting global supply chains, posing significant risks at critical chokepoints. Strong substitution effects and the use of inventories have helped to mitigate adverse output effects of chokepoint disruptions, but they often come at the cost of higher input prices. An effective policy response to chokepoint disruptions requires a tailored approach that takes account of the cause, centrality and the private sector’s ability to substitute and draw on buffers.

title: Money and the architecture of trust
raw_summary: Money is one of the most consequential social institutions humanity has built. Starting from the most elementary monetary act, a payment, this paper provides an account of how money works, grounded in the tradition of credit theories of money.

title: Are stablecoins and bank deposits substitutes?
raw_summary: We test whether stablecoins and bank deposits act as substitutes by estimating the semi-elasticity of stablecoin market capitalization with respect to deposit rate changes. Using local projections fit to weekly U.S. data from January 2019 to June 2025, we find that deposit rate increases predict slower stablecoin growth. To address endogeneity, we exploit a nonlinearity in deposit rate pass-through.

title: Transformative AI and demand bottlenecks
raw_summary: Transformative AI promises to accelerate growth through productivity enhancement and automation. Yet automation on such a scale would raise the share of investment in output, potentially starving AI innovation of returns from a shrinking consumer market.

title: Artificial intelligence and climate change: balancing innovation and sustainability
raw_summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming an increasingly important factor in the climate transition. AI can improve energy efficiency, optimise resource use, accelerate climate innovation and strengthen climate forecasting, adaptation and risk management. At the same time, the development and deployment of AI require substantial computational resources, increasing electricity demand and, depending on the carbon intensity and timing of electricity use, associated emissions.

title: Chasing El Dorado: gold under shifting geopolitical and financial conditions

raw_summary: From the Great Recession until 2019, U.S. labor productivity growth disappointed. Nonfarm-business output per hour grew about 1 percent a year from 2010 to 2019, down from 3 percent in the late 1990s. This slowdown was especially pronounced in manufacturing, and it coincided with a slowdown in the growth of revenue per worker among public firms. However, since 2019, growth has picked up to twice the 2010s rate, around 2 percent. In this post, I use data from firms’ 10-K filings to unpack this recent acceleration. I first show that the acceleration appears in public firms’ revenue per worker, then document how the gains went into profit margins, and finally, what firm characteristics predicted significant profit margin increases. The increase in profit margins is consistent with ongoing declines in the labor share of output .

title: Has the AI Boom Impacted the U.S. Current Account?
raw_summary: The AI boom is showing up in different corners of the U.S. economy, including international trade. Imports of semiconductors, servers, and computing equipment have climbed sharply yet the U.S. current account deficit has been largely unchanged. To better understand how the AI boom has not substantially affected the trade balance, consider that the current account is dictated by the gap between domestic saving and investment spending. It turns out that aggregate saving and investment spending have not changed much during the AI boom. Aggregate investment has not risen due to weakness outside the AI sector and business saving has remained robust.

title: Prices, Prices, Prices: Overall Inflation and the Costs You Care About
raw_summary: As fall starts to show itself in cooler weather, I want to discuss a topic that usually raises temperatures: inflation. Like a budget-conscious consumer, the Federal Reserve is highly attuned to changes in the price of goods and services; minimizing such swings is one of the Fed’s primary duties, after all. But how does the Fed’s view of prices differ from that of a consumer? And how does the Fed go about stabilizing prices writ large when it lacks the ability to set prices directly? In this post, I explore that apparent paradox from the perspective of a central banker (though I remain a budget-conscious consumer when off duty).

title: AI Adoption and Employment Expectations: Evidence from a Survey of Small Business Owners
raw_summary: There is little consensus on the effect of AI adoption on employment. Economy-wide measures of pay and headcount have moved little even as AI adoption has spread rapidly, yet narrower measures document declining hiring for workers at the start of their careers or in AI-exposed occupations . In this post, we revisit this topic for U.S. small businesses. We use data from the 2025 Small Business Credit Survey (SBCS) to examine the twelve-month-forward employment and revenue expectations of AI users. We find that firms currently using AI are significantly more likely than non-users to expect increased employment and revenues over the next year, even after accounting for firm and owner characteristics and location. Revenue expectations are most optimistic for AI users that report facing operational challenges in utilizing technology.

title: Firm Heterogeneity and the Response of Investment to Monetary Policy
raw_summary: It is well known that monetary policy affects firms’ investment decisions. But which firms are the most responsive to changes in interest rates? And does this responsiveness vary over time? The literature has given diverse answers to this question, focusing on characteristics such as firm size, age, and financial position, and mostly studying these traits in isolation. In this post based on a recent Staff Report , we explore how investment responsiveness to monetary policy changes across firms and over time. We find that investment by most firms in most time periods responds little to monetary policy. For some firms in some periods, however, investment is very responsive to changes in interest rates. While these instances of strong sensitivity correlate with several firm traits, there is substantial variation that cannot easily be linked to specific characteristics of firms. Our findings therefore underscore the importance of considering the entire distribution of investment responses rather than focusing on the average effect.

title: How Fast Do Tariffs Pass Through into Consumer Prices?
raw_summary: There has been a lot of interest in how tariffs affect consumer prices (for example, Cavallo et al. 2021 , 2025 ). In this post, we present results from our new research paper that estimates the effects of the 2025-26 tariffs on retail consumer prices. We find that for every percentage point increase in average tariffs, consumer goods prices increase by about a quarter of a percent after one year. Roughly two-thirds of the effect arises because tariffs raise the prices of imported consumer goods. The remaining third arises indirectly: tariffs increase the prices of goods made in the U.S. because producers pay more for imported parts and materials, and because producers raise their markups when competing imports cost more. The effects differ in their timing. Prices of imported goods respond quickly to tariffs, while prices of U.S.-made goods adjust over six to twelve months as higher costs move through the supply chain.

title: FEDS Paper: A Macroeconomic Analysis of Household Labor Supply Responses to Large Fiscal Transfers
raw_summary: Isabel Cairó , Shigeru Fujita, and Camilo Morales-Jimenez The fiscal transfers deployed during the COVID-19 pandemic were unprecedented in scale and strongly progressive. Using CPS/ASEC data, we document that the decline in employment during the pandemic was larger for low-income households and tightly linked to the intensity of transfer receipt, a pattern absent during the Global Financial Crisis. We develop and estimate a two-sector, heterogeneous-household general equilibrium model in which low-income households are borrowing-constrained in normal times but can save out of sufficiently large transfers. Because preferences permit wealth effects on labor supply, transfers both reduce labor supply and raise consumption, and a dollar of transfers is split roughly evenly between the two margins. We find that the effects of transfers are state-dependent: because the borrowing constraint binds more tightly in a deeper recession, the same transfer relaxes a tighter constraint and delivers an employment and consumption response about 40 to 50 percent larger during the pandemic than when the same transfer is introduced in the steady state. In the model, transfers were welfare-improving for recipients, with gains diminishing as transfers increase.

title: FEDS Paper: Inattentive Price Setting and Inflation Under Fiscal Policy Uncertainty
raw_summary: Oliver Pfäuti and Edson Wu How do high public debt and fiscal uncertainty interact to shape inflation? We develop a model in which firms face uncertainty about both marginal costs and fiscal policy and choose how much information to acquire before setting prices. Higher debt raises steady-state taxes, affecting attention through two opposing forces. While these taxes reduce the profit stakes of mispricing, they make desired prices more sensitive to tax fluctuations, increasing the value of information. The interaction generates a U-shaped relationship between public debt and attention, and therefore between debt and inflation volatility. Using euro-area firm-level expectations data, we document that the passthrough of expected input-cost growth into expected selling-price growth rises systematically with a country's debt-to-GDP ratio, consistent with the model. In the calibrated general-equilibrium model, an increase in debt from 100% to 175% of GDP raises inflation volatility by about 20%, mainly because firms reallocate attention toward fiscal shocks.

title: Operational excellence in serverless — 5E’s framework
raw_summary: Transform serverless freedom into business agility through the 5E’s framework: empower, engineer, evaluate, evolve and enhance. Modern digital businesses need software systems that are agile, reliable and cost-efficient. At Capital One, we’ve adopted a serverless-first approach to transform how we build and deploy applications, trading server management for a focus on delivering business value. While this paradigm eliminates operational overhead related to infrastructure, it doesn’t eliminate the need for operational excellence. In fact, the distributed, event-driven nature of serverless systems introduces a new set of challenges. When looking to achieve operational excellence in serverless systems, organizations must require disciplined engineering-automation, observability, cost control and a culture of continuous improvement. Understanding operational excellence in the serverless context Operational excellence focuses on how cloud systems are designed, deployed, monitored and optimized for long-term performance and reliability. In a serverless context, it involves: Automation : infrastructure and deployment as code Resilience : designing for failures, timeouts and throttling from day one Observability : collecting logs, metrics and traces across functions and services Cost visibility : paying only for what’s used, while avoiding hidden inefficiencies Continuous improvement : using data and feedback to refine architecture Serverless architecture can reduce reliance on infrastructure management, but it necessitates robust operational discipline to effectively handle distributed workloads. We will now delve into the five guiding principles, known as the 5E’s, which bridge the gap between operational excellence and practical engineering practices. Figure 1: Operational excellence illustrative architecture — The 5E’s Framework for Resilience & Agility Empower: automation and governance Empowerment starts with automation and clarity. Teams must have the freedom to deploy quickly while maintaining consistent operational standards. Engineering practices In practice, this balance is achieved through a core set of engineering practices: Infrastructure as code (IaC) : Use tools such as Terraform, Bicep or CloudFormation to version and review infrastructure changes. Continuous integration/continuous delivery (CI/CD) : Automate builds, tests and rollouts. Integrate static analysis and policy checks early. Policy as code : Apply guardrails for compliance and security directly in pipelines. Self-service deployment : Encourage “You build it, you run it” ownership with automated rollbacks and clear operational visibility. When developers are empowered through automation and safe defaults, organizations gain velocity without sacrificing control. Engineer: reliability, scalability and observability Engineering excellence is the foundation of operational maturity. In serverless environments, systems must be resilient, observable and scalable by design. Reliability patterns These patterns help serverless systems recover gracefully when things inevitably go wrong: Design idempotent functions to handle retries gracefully. Implement dead-letter queues (DLQs) for unprocessed events. Use managed workflow orchestration (e.g., Step Functions, Durable Functions or Workflows) to manage dependencies. Practice fault injection or chaos testing to validate recovery strategies. Scalability and performance These practices keep serverless systems fast and elastic as demand fluctuates: Adopt asynchronous eventing to decouple workloads. Use caching and edge delivery for latency-sensitive paths. Profile cold-start latency and optimize initialization logic. Observability These practices ensure teams can trace, measure and troubleshoot behavior across every function: Collect metrics, logs and traces across all functions. Correlate requests using trace IDs for end-to-end visibility. Build dashboards for throughput, errors and cost per invocation. By engineering observability and reliability into every function, teams can turn runtime behavior into actionable insights. Evaluate: measure what matters Operational excellence is measurable. Success should be based on objective signals, not assumptions. Here are some of the many metrics one might track: These dashboards are made visible within our engineering organization to create shared ownership. When teams track performance and cost together, they discover insights that help them balance agility and efficiency. Evolve: continuous optimization No architecture is ever “done.” Workloads, dependencies and customer expectations evolve, and your systems must evolve with them. Technical optimizations These optimizations keep infrastructure aligned with how the system actually runs, not how it was originally designed: Review usage patterns to tune memory, time-outs and concurrency. Migrate synchronous flows to event-driven designs for elasticity. Automate patching and runtime upgrades through IaC pipelines. Refactor high-cost or underperforming functions using data from cost and performance reports. Process evolution We cultivate an environment where reflection and adjustment happen as routinely as deployment: Schedule quarterly operational reviews focused on metrics, not just code. Introduce internal “learning sprints” where teams analyze incidents and share optimizations. Operational excellence thrives when teams treat every deployment as an opportunity to learn and refine. Enhance: feedback and learning loops The final step is enhancement, turning data into continuous improvement. Operational excellence isn’t static; it’s sustained through learning loops that connect incidents, telemetry and process improvements. Best practices Closing the loop between incidents and improvement comes down to a few key best practices: Conduct blameless postmortems after incidents and feed actions back into code or pipeline rules. Automate alerts for anomaly detection and integrate them with collaboration tools. Align retrospectives around measurable operational KPIs, not just delivery velocity. Reinforce psychological safety. Improvement happens when teams feel safe to surface failures early. Enhancement ensures that excellence becomes a habit, not a one-time achievement. Points to remember Pulling these ideas together, a few key takeaways stand out: Culture and empowerment : Great architecture stems from an empowered team, not just tools. By automating routine workflows, we empower developers to focus on higher-level problem-solving, reinforcing that automation is a partner to human ingenuity, not a replacement. Metrics and customer impact : Use metrics like latency, reliability and cost to gain clarity, always linking them back to how they affect the customer. Visibility and trust: Foster trust by making operational data accessible to everyone. Automation and innovation : Automation frees up time from manual tasks, allowing for greater innovation and improvement. Continuous learning and reliability : Sustain reliability through ongoing evolution of architecture, processes and people. Conclusion Serverless technology frees engineers from infrastructure, but operational excellence transforms that freedom into business agility. It’s not just about scaling code; it’s about scaling learning. By empowering teams with automation, engineering for resilience, evaluating what matters, evolving with data and enhancing through feedback, we’re building cloud systems that are reliable, efficient and continually improving. Operational excellence isn’t a destination-it’s the rhythm of modern serverless architecture. Originally published at https://www.capitalone.com . The Mills ReviewThat is why we commissioned the Mills Review, published in July, focused on how AI could reshape retail financial services by 2030.Some developments we anticipated are already emerging, including the transition towards agentic finance, such as the launch of Meta’s Muse.Our response to the review is not to consult, study and report progress.Our focus is testing, assurance, monitoring and surveillance: directly with industry to understand how AI systems are being deployed.Whilst the Review focused on retail, the AI shift does not stop at the retail boundary.Across wholesale markets too, AI is accelerating how firms analyse, trade, monitor and make decisions.We are embedding 6 of the 7 recommendations into live work immediately. Our innovation services such as the AI Lab give us direct insight into what firms are building from agent-led payments and fraud detection to consumer support.On frontier AI security, we are working directly with banks to understand how frontier models are changing cyber defence, identifying and linking vulnerabilities and assisting with triaging, patching and recovering at greater speed. Those insights are feeding directly into our supervisory and policy response.Firms are not bystanders in that process. The leaders will be those that deploy AI effectively, innovatively and safely.But increasingly, AI is also changing what happens before a consumer ever reaches a regulated firm. Consumers are turning to general-purpose large language models (LLMs), like ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude, for financial information and advice, while regulated firms are beginning to integrate their services into AI platforms.The good news – this can significantly widen access to financial tools and information. But it can also blur the boundary between regulated and unregulated activity, and the protections consumers receive.Four in five less-experienced investors aged 18-40 have used AI to help with investing, but only 40% of consumers correctly recognise that there is no recourse if something goes wrong after acting on advice from a general-purpose AI tool. Our answer is not simply to expand our remit, but to make the existing boundary clearer.Through InvestSmart and the FCA Firm Checker, we already help consumers understand the protections they have. But warnings may be more effective at the point where AI-generated financial information is delivered.So we are calling on AI providers to help consumers understand the limits of financial information and advice generated by their models through clear, proportionate and consistent disclaimers.And rather than create a new public-interest financial capability tool, as the Mills Review suggested, we will build on existing work, including IOSCO’s first TechSprint, powered by our AI Lab to help investors spot scams, verify information and challenge unreliable AI outputs.
